docs.title: qcdata
docs.text: Data structures for quantum chemistry inputs and results, with Jupyter visualizations.

docs.title: The QC Suite
docs.text:
These packages work together to make quantum chemistry fast, structured, and interoperable.

  • qcref - Reference data for computational chemistry: CODATA physical constants, conversion factors, a periodic table, and solvent properties, each value with its source.
  • qcdata - Data structures for quantum chemistry inputs and results, with Jupyter visualizations. Documentation
  • qcinf - Cheminformatics algorithms and structure utilities for qcdata structures.
  • qccompute - Runs programs on qcdata inputs, one calculation or many, in this process or in workers, with an optional store, and returns structured results. Documentation
  • qccodec - The optional add-on for external programs (ORCA, Psi4, xtb, CREST, ...): writes their native inputs, runs them and parses their outputs, registering each as a program qccompute runs. Documentation
  • qcstore - Keeps results under their calculation key: immutable runs, tags, and an optional index.
  • BigChem - Distributed execution of qccompute calculations across clusters of computers or the cloud.
  • ChemCloud - A web application and Python client that expose a BigChem cluster securely over the internet.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
These pages document the next release, which is in alpha. Install it with minimum versions (--prerelease=allow lets the resolver take pre-releases):

uv pip install --prerelease=allow "qcdata>=0.24.0a8"

With the visualizations (view extra), or with the packages that run programs and store results:

uv pip install --prerelease=allow "qcdata[view]>=0.24.0a8" "qcinf>=0.6.0a2"
uv pip install --prerelease=allow "qcdata>=0.24.0a8" "qccompute[qccodec]>=0.23.0a6" "qccodec>=0.22.0a5" "qcstore>=0.1.0a4"

The alpha's documentation is at qcdata.docs.afh.org/next, the stable release's at qcdata.docs.afh.org.

The stable release, for a minimal installation:

python -m pip install qcdata

To install all extra feature such as cheminformatics and visualization tools:

python -m pip install qcdata[all]

You may need to put '' around the brackets in some terminals

python -m pip install 'qcdata[all]'

docs.title: ✨ Visualization ✨
docs.text:
Visualize all your results with a single line of code!

First install the visualization module:

python -m pip install qcdata[view]

or if your shell requires '' around arguments with brackets:

python -m pip install 'qcdata[view]'

Then in a Jupyter notebook import the qcdata view module and call view.view(...) passing it one or any number of qcdata objects you want to visualize, including Structure objects or any ProgramOutput object. You may also pass an array of titles and/or subtitles to add additional information to the molecular structure display. If no titles are passed qcdata will look for Structure identifiers such as a name or SMILES to label the Structure.

Seamless visualizations for ProgramOutput objects make results analysis easy!

Single point calculations display their results in a table.

If you want to use the HTML generated by the viewer to build your own dashboards use the functions inside of qcdata.view.py that begin with the word generate_ to create HTML you can insert into any dashboard.

Check out the API Documentation to understand how qcdata works. Take a look at the Visualizations to see how easy it is to understand your results using qcdata!

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: The names, units and rules that every AFH program (axtb, qcopt, ...) and every qc* codec share, so that inputs look alike and outputs can be read the same way whichever program produced them. This page is the single place for them; a program's own documentation covers only what is specific to it. How programs are run (the program and session protocol, plans, workers) is qccompute's: see its program interface design.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Atomic units at every interface: energies in hartree (Eh), positions in bohr, gradients in Eh/bohr, Hessians in Eh/bohr², dipole moments in e·bohr, quadrupole moments in e·bohr², polarizabilities in e²·bohr²/Eh. A field or key whose name says otherwise (memory_gib) is in that unit. Chemistry's fixed conventions are kept where every program prints them:

quantity unit frequencies, rotational constants cm⁻¹ (imaginary frequencies negative) masses u force constants mdyn/Å IR intensities km/mol temperatures, pressures, concentrations K, Pa, mol/L entropies, heat capacities Eh/K times wall-clock seconds memory GiB (2³⁰ bytes)

XYZ files are read and written in Å.

docs.title: Settings (ProgramInput.keywords)
docs.text:
keywords is the program's own settings tree, exactly as its JSON request file and its Python keyword arguments spell it. The rules:

  1. Every setting is group.key or a top-level scalar, never deeper. A key never repeats its group's name (solvent.name, not solvent.solvent).
  2. One canonical spelling across the CLI, JSON, Python and qcdata. Synonyms that encode another program's vocabulary (rijcosx, rhf) may be accepted on input but are never echoed back. A group may take a scalar that stands for its main key (a DFT program's jk: "df" is {"kind": "df"}); the schema shows both forms and resolved.settings reports the expanded one. The calculation key takes the input as given, so the two forms are separate cache entries: callers that store results use one.
  3. "auto" means the program decides; null or absent means the default. Every output reports what each auto became in resolved.settings, and why in resolved.reasons.
  4. Tolerances end in _tol, iteration limits are max_iter, units appear in names only exactly (memory_gib). Booleans only for two-state choices.
  5. Every setting given must affect the calculation. Unknown keys, settings that do not apply to the calculation type, and settings made irrelevant by other values are errors of kind input (codes unknown_key, not_applicable, no_effect), with a did-you-mean suggestion where one exists. Contingent settings, which apply only if something happens during the run (an SOSCF or escalation threshold, a stability probe's gap, a level shift), are allowed; the run's record says whether each one fired. A session checks its keywords against the calculation types it was opened for (open_session(..., calctypes=...)), and a request of another type fails with not_applicable.
  6. Each program publishes the JSON Schema of its settings (settings_schema(calctype)), with x-unit, x-tier (common, expert), x-concern (model, approximation, convergence, algorithm, resource, output) and x-applies-to on every key.
  7. model.method and model.basis carry the method and basis; structure carries positions, atoms, charge and multiplicity. The settings tree does not repeat them.
  8. keywords hold plain JSON. A pydantic model given in them, at any depth (an Accuracy), is stored as its JSON form with nulls left out, so an input saves, reloads and keys the same.

docs.title: Shared names
docs.text:
Settings that mean the same in several programs are spelled the same:

key meaning threads CPU threads the calculation may use memory_gib memory the calculation may use (GiB) backend cpu, gpu or auto device_memory_gib GPU memory the calculation may use (GiB) accuracy the input's accuracy target: energy (Eh), gradient (Eh/bohr), hessian (Eh/bohr²) scf.max_iter, scf.e_tol, scf.g_tol, scf.guess SCF iteration limit, energy and orbital-gradient tolerances, starting guess solvent.name, solvent.model, solvent.eps implicit solvent: name, continuum model, permittivity freq.temperature, freq.pressure, freq.scale, freq.imaginary_cutoff thermochemistry conditions, frequency scale factor, imaginary-mode cutoff (cm⁻¹) output.orbitals, output.overlap, output.hamiltonian, output.core_hamiltonian, output.molden, output.bond_orders optional outputs: the wavefunction outputs by name; output.molden is off, spherical or cartesian and returns files["orbitals.molden"] convergence.max_iter, convergence.g_tol, convergence.e_tol, convergence.d_tol geometry optimizer convergence

A program that cannot honour a shared setting (axtb's SCF thresholds follow xtb's accuracy factor; its ALPB/GBSA models are parametrized per solvent name, so no solvent.eps) rejects it with kind unsupported rather than ignoring it.

Resource keys (threads, memory_gib, backend, device_memory_gib) carry x-concern: "resource". The calculation key leaves out threads, memory_gib and device_memory_gib, which change results at most at round-off; backend (which device runs the calculation) counts.

docs.title: Accuracy targets
docs.text:
accuracy is a JSON object of absolute targets, each optional: energy (Eh), gradient (Eh/bohr, the largest component) and hessian (Eh/bohr², the largest element), as in qcdata.Accuracy. It is never a bare number: it applies to every calctype a session runs, so a number would have no single quantity to aim at.

  • It is the input's own target: of compute, and of every session request that gives none. A request's accuracy replaces it for that request.
  • The program turns it into its own convergence thresholds and records the target, the thresholds and any error estimate under the record key accuracy. Explicit convergence settings are floors: a target may tighten them, never loosen them.
  • It is part of the input, so of the calculation key: a tighter target is another calculation.
  • A program with no convergence settings (a force field, an ML potential, a FunctionProgram) accepts a target, as the keyword or a session request's alike, and records it as met: no thresholds, and a convergence error of exactly zero for each target. So a session can pass a request's target on as the keyword.
  • A program whose convergence settings take no targets yet refuses a target with kind unsupported, like any shared setting it cannot honour.

The record of a target met with no thresholds, for {"gradient": 1e-6}:

"record": {"accuracy": {"target": {"gradient": 1e-06}, "thresholds": {},
                        "estimate": {"gradient": 0.0}}}

target holds the targets given, thresholds is empty, and estimate gives 0.0 for each target, so a reader checks any program the same way: each estimate at or below its target.

Accuracy.from_keywords(keywords) reads it the same way in every program, and refuses a bare number, an unknown key (unknown_key) and an object with no target (no_effect).

docs.title: Calculation key
docs.text:
A store files each result under qcdata.calculation_key(inp): k1: followed by the sha256 hex digest of a canonical JSON text of the input as given, and nothing else. Two inputs share a key only when they request the same calculation written the same way. Every rule errs toward a miss, because a wrong hit returns another calculation's numbers.

The canonical text is the input's canonical form, written as compact JSON (separators , and :), keys sorted, non-ASCII characters escaped as \uXXXX, with:

  • numbers normalized: a float with an integral value is written as an integer (100.0 as 100, -0.0 as 0), any other float in Python's shortest round-trip form (1e-08), integers exactly. true and 1 stay distinct. Non-finite numbers are refused;
  • fields at their default left out (charge: 0, keywords: {}, basis: null), so adding a field to qcdata never changes an old key. Inside keywords nothing is a default: values stay as given, nulls and empty groups included;
  • coordinates of structure and of every structure in structures: bohr times 10¹⁰, rounded to integers (half to even), atom order kept. Symbols, charge, multiplicity and connectivity count as given;
  • every other array field (a given Hessian, orbital coefficients) as {"array": shape, "dtype": "float64", "sha256": digest}, the digest of its C-order little-endian float64 bytes with -0.0 as 0.0. The digest tells values apart exactly as their JSON numbers would, at a small fraction of the cost. Integer arrays enter the same way in their own dtype. Non-finite values are refused;
  • files (of the input, of each subprogram and of given) by the sha256 hex digest of their bytes, text as UTF-8;
  • subprograms canonicalized the same way, in order;
  • tuples as lists; numpy arrays and scalars inside free-form values (keywords) as JSON numbers, as they are once saved.

Left out: extras at every level, structure identifiers, and the resource keywords threads, memory_gib and device_memory_gib at the top level of keywords, in the input and in every subprogram (scf.threads would count). These three may change results at most at round-off. Everything else counts: given, cmdline_args, and settings such as backend (pinning the device), precision and accuracy that can change numbers.

Spellings are not normalized. B3LYP and b3lyp, a synonym, a group's scalar and expanded forms (rule 2), a default written out (scf.max_iter: 100), and null against an absent key all give different keys: a cache miss, never a wrong hit. The key normalizes only itself; stored values keep -0.0 and their number types.

The key names the calculation, never the code that produced its numbers. Which code did is each program's numerics identity (its version, or a numerics epoch, an executable's version, a model's checksum), which the runner and the store record with every run, for the input's program and each subprogram, and which every output carries in execution.identities. A store keeps several runs per key and reuses one only when its identities match the programs that would run now. So a key never changes when code changes, anything holding keys stays valid across releases, and computing a key never needs a program installed. A program that changes what a default computes (a DFT program's jk defaulting to df) changes its numerics identity, not the key.

Golden keys in qcdata's tests pin the canonical form. Changing any rule, the default of any field an input holds (an omitted field would then mean something else), or the type of a field between a list of numbers and an array (list[float] and a digest enter differently) is a new key version, k2, released deliberately.

docs.title: Calculation types
docs.text:
energy, gradient, hessian, and the types made of many evaluations (optimization, transition_state, irc, path_optimization, conformer_search, ...), usually run by a program with subprograms. A hessian result also holds the energy and gradient at the same geometry and, when the program can make them, the harmonic analysis (vibrational_analysis) and thermochemistry (thermochemistry), tuned or switched off with freq.*.

results.hessian is the full Cartesian second derivative of the energy at the input geometry, never projected. Hessians are used away from stationary points (the start of a transition-state search, an IRC's updates), where the gradient gives rotations a part in the Hessian that projecting them out would lose. Only translational invariance holds exactly, and that is physics, not projection. Projection belongs to the harmonic analysis, which records what it projected (VibrationalAnalysis.projection). A program whose underlying code projects the Hessian undoes the projection (from the gradient and the rigid-body modes, or by reading an unprojected matrix the code also writes), or refuses with kind unsupported where it cannot: at a geometry whose gradient is not zero, the projection changed the matrix.

docs.title: Standard fields first
docs.text: A quantity two programs report goes into a typed field, never into extras. extras is for what has no standard home yet.

docs.title: energy_components
docs.text:
A partition of energy: the values add up to it. Standard keys:

key term nuclear_repulsion nuclear repulsion one_electron kinetic and nuclear attraction (plus ECPs) coulomb electron-electron Coulomb exchange exact exchange xc exchange-correlation functional (semilocal) vv10 VV10 nonlocal correlation dispersion empirical dispersion (D3, D4) solvation_electrostatic continuum solvation, electrostatic solvation_cds SMD cavity-dispersion-solvent structure electronic tight-binding electronic energy repulsion tight-binding or force-field repulsion electrostatic, hydrogen_bond, halogen_bond further tight-binding and force-field terms

What a component contains is the program's: GFN2-xTB's electronic is not g-xTB's. A program with a hierarchy of overlapping terms reports the partition here and the hierarchy in record.

docs.title: Shared record keys
docs.text:
record is shaped by each program's record schema. A few keys mean the same in every program that reports them:

key type meaning warm_start bool or null on a session frame: the calculation started from its lineage's history (previous orbitals, charges, probe state), not from the input alone, so it can reach a different solution than a fresh calculation; null when the method keeps no lineage state (GFN-FF). Programs add their own detail beside it (a DFT program: where the SCF guess came from, and the lineage it was seeded from) accuracy object on a calculation with an accuracy target (the keyword's or a request's): target (the targets as resolved: energy, gradient, hessian), thresholds (the program's own convergence thresholds used, under its own names; empty for a program with none) and, where the program has one, estimate (an error estimate per field; 0.0 for each target of a program with no convergence settings)

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text:
Fields whose meaning depends on a scheme name it beside them:

field kind field values atomic_charges atomic_charges_kind mulliken, lowdin, eeq, eeqbc, cm5, hirshfeld atomic_spin_populations atomic_spin_populations_kind those of atomic_charges_kind bond_orders bond_orders_kind mayer (Σ(PS)μν(PS)νμ; what xtb prints as "Wiberg"), wiberg (orthogonalized basis)

Fields with one definition have no kind:

  • dipole_moment and quadrupole_moment are the moments of the method's charge distribution, electrons and nuclei, whatever the method: an SCF density, a force field's or tight-binding model's charges (GFN-FF's EEQ charges), an ML potential's prediction. The quadrupole is Buckingham's traceless tensor, ½Σq(3rᵢrⱼ − r²δᵢⱼ) about the coordinate origin. tblite's molecular quadrupole, which the g-xTB 2.0.1 program prints, counts the off-diagonal charge and dipole parts twice and is not a tensor.
  • atomic_dipoles and atomic_quadrupoles are electronic only, about each atom's nucleus: μ_A = −Σ_{μ∈A}(P D)_μμ, with the integrals about the atom of the column AO; quadrupoles in Buckingham's traceless form, 3/2 M − 1/2 tr(M) I, 3 × 3 per atom.
  • shell_populations are electron populations Σ_{μ∈shell}(PS)_μμ, indexed like basis.shells, with shell_atoms and shell_angular_momenta beside them; not charges.

docs.title: Imaginary modes
docs.text: Frequencies are negative for imaginary modes and stored without a cutoff; VibrationalAnalysis.n_imaginary(cutoff) applies one (xtb and axtb use 20 cm⁻¹).

docs.title: Orbitals and AO matrices
docs.text:
Orbitals is the one home of orbital levels. Energies and occupations come with every wavefunction; coefficients only on request. Occupations are per spin, each between 0 and 1, with both occupations_a and occupations_b always given; electronic_temperature is 0 for aufbau occupations, and smeared ones carry a Fermi level per spin, except for a spin that holds no electrons (a smeared H atom's beta), which has none. Orbitals.core_electrons counts, per atom, the electrons the orbitals do not represent (ECP cores, or the core a valence-only method leaves out; None for an all-electron calculation), so the occupations sum to Σ(Z − core_electrons) − charge. An ECP carries the core it replaces (Ecp.core_electrons), and the two agree on every ECP atom.

The coefficients and the AO matrices are indexed by the AOs of one basis set, Wavefunction.basis, present whenever any of them is and only then: an overlap alone ships the basis set and no coefficients. They are stored as the program produced them, with the basis set's AOConvention; Wavefunction.with_convention converts them all together. The default is PySCF's (libcint's) order: spherical functions m = −l..l except p as (x, y, z); Cartesian components lexicographic (xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz); every spherical function and the x^l component unit-normalized. A change of Cartesian normalization scales coefficients by s per AO, densities by s_μ s_ν and operators (overlap, hamiltonian_a/_b, core_hamiltonian) by 1/(s_μ s_ν); BasisSet.transform takes the array's kind and never guesses it.

docs.title: Wavefunction outputs
docs.text:
The optional parts of SinglePointData.wavefunction are requested by name, in a session request's outputs or as the keyword output.<name>:

output adds implies orbitals Orbitals.coefficients_a/_b the basis set overlap Wavefunction.overlap the basis set hamiltonian Wavefunction.hamiltonian_a/_b overlap, orbitals core_hamiltonian Wavefunction.core_hamiltonian the basis set

The basis set (Wavefunction.basis) is not an output of its own: it comes with any of the four, since it describes the AO space they share. A program fills in what an output implies instead of refusing it, since requesting an output changes no other number. It refuses an output it cannot give with kind unsupported, code not_applicable, and a message naming the reason: a mode whose last diagonalization is not of one build refuses hamiltonian; a force field has none of the four. There is no density output: the SCF density is Orbitals.density().

docs.title: Given results
docs.text:
ProgramInput.given holds results already known at the input's structure (a SinglePointData). It is a record of what is known, not a setting, so the strict rule for settings (rule 5) applies to it differently:

  • A program uses the fields it can and records each one it used in resolved (hessian.initial: "given", scf.guess: "given"). Fields it does not use, descriptive ones included (calcinfo_*, scf_iterations, energy_components), are left alone, so given=frame.results works as it stands.
  • Given values are starting points, never results: a program does not report a given value as its own (qcopt computes the energy and gradient at a given TS and takes only the Hessian). provenance names the producing program and version only, so reusing a value as a result could silently mix methods (GFN2 and g-xTB are both "axtb").
  • It refuses the input (kind input, code not_applicable) when it can use none of the fields, or when a field it would use does not fit: other atoms (qcdata checks shapes), another basis for a wavefunction. A starting guess needs no match of program or method: a GFN2 Hessian is a sound initial Hessian for a DFT transition-state search.
  • Checking the model is the caller's, which knows the producing input (qcopt.irc(ts_out) passes the search's Hessian only when its spec matches).

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text:
ProgramWarning(code, message, path): code is stable snake_case; path is the dotted settings key concerned, if any. Settings problems are errors, not warnings (rule 5), so warnings report what happened during a run (a fallback taken, a probe fired, slow convergence). Shared codes:

code meaning deprecated_key after a program's 1.0, an old key still accepted for a stated period; the message names the new one. Before 1.0 a program rejects old keys (unknown_key) instead resource_capped a resource request in the keywords (threads, memory_gib, ...) above what the runner granted; the program used the grant (it uses the smaller of request and grant, or the grant alone when nothing was requested) backend_fallback the calculation ran on another backend than first chosen (a GPU out of memory, so the CPU), which backend: auto allows; an explicit backend fails instead loosely_converged an iterative procedure (an SCF, response equations) missed its thresholds and was accepted under a relaxed rule (a stalled SCF accepted on an energy plateau, ORCA's continuation after "near convergence"). The message gives the residual reached and the rule that accepted it; path names the threshold missed (scf.g_tol), if it is a setting. Without this warning a success met its thresholds

Programs define further codes in their own documentation.

Shared error codes (kind input):

code meaning unknown_key not a setting of this program not_applicable a setting of another calculation type, or a session request outside the calctypes it was opened for. With kind unsupported, an optional output the program cannot give no_effect made irrelevant by the other values given not_modeled the structure's charge or multiplicity is one the method does not represent (GFN-FF given a radical, a neutral-only ML potential given an ion). The message names the property. A method never runs on, or silently ignores, a charge or multiplicity it cannot model unnamed_subprogram a calculation ran, through its context (ctx.compute, ctx.session), a program its input does not name among its subprograms (recursively); the message names it. Refused so that a run's identities cover every program it used

Shared error codes of other kinds, which runners, schedulers and retrying workflows act on:

kind code meaning resource host_memory out of host memory (a failed allocation, or the plan's need above the grant); details as below resource device_memory out of GPU memory; details as below backend device_lost a GPU fault poisoned the device context (illegal address, launch failure, device assert, ECC error, launch timeout); nothing more can run in this process. A worker answers the request in flight with it and then exits; in process, the caller should not use the program again convergence scf_not_converged the SCF ended without meeting its thresholds (out of iterations, or stalled with no rule to accept it). The results hold the last iterate: its energy and, where the program gives them, its orbitals; the record holds what the program keeps of its history convergence response_not_converged the response equations (CPHF/CPKS, for a Hessian or a property) ended above their tolerance; the results reached are attached environment worker_died a worker process ended mid-request (a crash, a signal, an out-of-memory kill); set by the client, with the exit status and the tail of the worker's stderr in the message. A worker that exits on purpose answers the request in flight first (device_lost), so only later requests see worker_died

ErrorInfo.details holds structured facts about a failure as plain JSON, so a caller never parses the message. For host_memory and device_memory the keys are, each given when the program knows it, in the terms of the memory keyword (memory_gib for host memory, device_memory_gib for a device's):

key meaning required_gib the keyword's value (GiB) with which the calculation would fit: at least, when the program knows only that the failed allocation did not fit available_gib the keyword's value (GiB) the calculation ran with: the keyword as given, else the grant, else what the device had free

These are what a caller sets, not raw needs. A program that budgets only part of its memory (a DFT program that keeps a share for its workspaces) converts its need: a 3-index tensor of 1.25 GiB under a budget of 75% of memory_gib gives required_gib 1.67. The raw need, where useful, goes under a program key beside them.

{"kind": "resource", "code": "host_memory",
 "message": "RI-K needs at least 1.25 GiB for its 3-index exchange tensor, which takes memory_gib >= 1.67; it ran with 1.5",
 "details": {"required_gib": 1.67, "available_gib": 1.5, "tensor_gib": 1.25}}

A dispatcher that resubmits with memory_gib (or device_memory_gib) set to required_gib gets past this failure; qc* itself still schedules nothing by memory. Programs may add their own keys beside these, and other codes may define theirs.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
ErrorInfo(kind, message, code, program, cause, details), on failed outputs only. Kinds:

kind meaning input settings or a structure the program cannot run as given unsupported a valid request the program does not implement, or a setting it cannot honour convergence an iterative procedure did not converge (results so far attached) numerical non-finite values, singular matrices resource not enough memory or another resource as set up backend the hardware backend failed program a subprogram failed; cause holds its error timeout out of time (set by the runner) stopped the program stopped on request at one of its steps, its partial output attached (see Stopping) environment the program could not run: not installed, no licence, process died (set by the runner) internal a failure nobody anticipated: a bug (an exception other than ProgramError, a broken invariant, a crash) or, on the codec path, a failure no rule classifies (a reported failure, an unexplained exit, unreadable output). A failure a program or codec anticipates takes the kind that fits it

code refines a kind with a name callers can branch on: a shared code above, else the program's own. An optimizer's convergence failures keep their own codes (qcopt: max_iter, energy_rose, not_first_order_saddle, irc_incomplete); an SCF's and a response's are the shared scf_not_converged and response_not_converged, whichever program runs them.

A failed calculation raises ProgramError, from every program's compute and every session call alike, carrying its ErrorInfo and the partial results; any other exception is a bug. A program whose result is one output attaches it whole, ProgramError(out.error, output=out), so a trajectory's frames, record and resolved settings reach the caller as exc.output; a failed session step attaches its frame. A runner turns the exception into a failed ProgramOutput only where it needs data (a store, the outputs of a list, a worker's reply).

A program reports any failure of a subprogram as kind program, whether the subprogram's plan refused its settings or its run failed. program names the subprogram, cause holds the subprogram's own ErrorInfo, and the message starts with the subprogram and calctype (xtb (gradient): ...). Callers follow cause to the first error that is not of kind program to learn what went wrong. A subprogram that fails for one task of a round (a session that will not open, a failed request) fails that task only. A Python callable standing in for a subprogram (qcopt's in-process evaluator) is reported the same way, with program None. Its ProgramError gives the cause; any other exception becomes a cause of kind internal, as qccompute treats a program's bug.

docs.title: Timings and provenance
docs.text: execution.timings holds seconds per phase (total for the whole call; a program with subprograms adds subprograms, the time inside them). results.provenance names the program, program_version and program_commit. execution.identities says which code made the results: {program: numerics} for the input's program and each subprogram it names, as the runner saw them when it ran (a program named with several specs joins its sorted, distinct identities with ;). The runner sets it on every output it returns and the store keeps it with the run, so an output read back from a store names its code without a second lookup; a carried result keeps the identities that made it. An output a store holds names its run in execution.store_run, "<key>/<run>": the store sets it on every output it returns, and a runner sets it on an output it has just stored; it is never stored itself, and it is None on an output no store holds. An output of a batch also has timings["batch"], the whole batch's wall time (s), set by the runner; its wall_time is its own where the program can tell (a lockstep batch knows when each task finished), else the batch's.

docs.title: Progress events
docs.text: A program reports what it is doing through its runner context, ctx.progress(event), when the caller listens (it is None otherwise). An event is a small JSON object of the program's own (plain JSON values, in the units above, small enough to send every step), with one shared key: event, a snake_case name of what happened (step). Programs document their events. The runner adds path, the program names from the caller's input down to the program that emitted it; programs do not set it. Events are not results: nothing in them is stored, and no output depends on whether anyone listened.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
A caller may ask a running calculation to stop at its next step (qccompute's runner.stop(future)), to keep what it has reached: a search's frames so far, to analyze now. The program sees the request as ctx.stop_requested(), checks it where it can end cleanly (an optimizer: before each step), and ends there: its output is a failure of kind stopped with the partial results, raised as for any failure (ProgramError(out.error, output=out)). The request covers the whole calculation: a program whose subprogram stopped stops too, with kind stopped rather than program. A program with no steps to stop at need not check, and runs to its end.

A stopped output is where the caller chose to end the run, not what the input gives: a runner never stores one, and a store never reuses one.

docs.title: Saved files
docs.text:
save writes a model as JSON, YAML or TOML. Indented JSON (the default, indent=4) keeps each innermost array, a list holding no lists or objects, on one line, so a structure's coordinates read as one row per atom:

"geometry": [
    [-8.601339697312277, -0.6368849812267334, 0.7906010193844016],
    [-6.3155913218934, 0.4215960361624519, 1.2240196532066823]
]

An array field whose float64 size exceeds 1 MiB (more than 131,072 numbers) goes to its own .npy file beside the saved file, named by the file's stem and the array's path in the document, and the document holds a pointer in its place:

"hessian": {"path": "output.results.hessian.npy", "shape": [480, 480],
            "dtype": "float64", "sha256": "..."}

sha256 is the digest of the .npy file's bytes. Path parts other than letters, digits, _ and - are written as %XX (a structure role qm.mm gives structures.qm%2Emm.geometry). open reads every array back and checks its digest, shape and dtype, so models always hold arrays and no field is a file reference. save returns every file it wrote, the model's file first. Smaller arrays and free-form values (extras, record) stay in the document, where JSON and YAML keep every float exactly; TOML loses the sign of -0.0.

A text in files whose UTF-8 size exceeds 1 MiB (a Molden or cube file, a long log) goes beside the saved file the same way: its UTF-8 bytes, named by the stem and its path in the document with no suffix added, and a pointer of its path and the file's sha256 in its place:

"files": {"orbitals.molden": {"path": "output.results.files.orbitals%2Emolden",
                              "sha256": "..."}}

open reads it back and checks the digest. Binary files stay in the document, base64 encoded.

docs.title: Why qcdata?
docs.text:
Other data structure package for quantum chemistry exist such as QCElemental and Atomic Simulation Environment. I often found these libraries were too heavy weight or too feature poor for most of what I needed. I also found their APIs to be somewhat unintuitive and often cumbersome to use. qcdata is designed to be easy to use, easy to reason about, and provide a unified format for diverse quantum chemistry calculations.

qcdata is also the central package used by qccompute to power interoperable quantum chemistry calculations across dozens of packages and bigchem, which scales QC calculations across hundreds of nodes on academic clusters or the cloud. I needed robust and reliable data structures for powering these applications. qcdata is the result of thousands of hours of organizing quantum chemistry data into coherent data structures.

It is my hope that you'll find qcdata to be intuitive and delightful to use. If you have any questions please open an issue on GitHub. Pull requests welcome :)

docs.title: qcdata.array_files
docs.text:
Large arrays and texts saved apart from a model's file, as files beside it.

Models always hold arrays; only saving decides where an array goes. An array field whose float64 size exceeds 1 MiB is written to its own .npy file in the saved file's directory, named by the saved file's stem and the array's path in the document (output.results.hessian.npy), and the document holds a pointer in its place:

{"path": "output.results.hessian.npy", "shape": [400, 400], "dtype": "float64",
 "sha256": "..."}

sha256 is the digest of the .npy file's bytes. Opening the file reads every array back, checking its digest, shape and dtype, so a loaded model holds arrays again. Only array fields (SerializableNDArray) are saved apart; free-form values such as extras and record stay inline.

A text in files whose UTF-8 size exceeds 1 MiB is saved apart the same way, when the sink is made with text_files=True (as QCDataBaseModel.save does): as its UTF-8 bytes, named by the stem and its path with no suffix added (output.results.files.orbitals%2Emolden), with {"path", "sha256"} in its place. Binary files stay inline.

QCDataBaseModel.save and QCDataBaseModel.open use this module, and any other writer of qcdata documents with arrays beside them (a worker's wire) can do the same:

from qcdata.array_files import DIRECTORY, SINK, ArraySink

sink = ArraySink()
document = model.model_dump(mode="json", context={SINK: sink})
document, written = sink.place(document, directory, stem)  # arrays to .npy files
model = type(model).model_validate(document, context={DIRECTORY: directory})

def add_text(self, text: str) -> str | dict[str, int]:
    """Hold a text over 1 MiB for its own file and return its mark; else the text.

    Args:
        text: The content of an entry of ``files``.

    Returns:
        The mark that takes the text's place, or the text itself when it stays
        inline (the sink saves no texts, or it is 1 MiB or less).
    """
    # Up to 4 UTF-8 bytes per character: only a text near the limit is encoded.
    if not self.text_files or len(text) * 4 <= ARRAY_FILE_BYTES:
        return text
    if len(text) <= ARRAY_FILE_BYTES and len(text.encode()) <= ARRAY_FILE_BYTES:
        return text
    self.texts.append(text)
    return {self.text_mark: len(self.texts) - 1}

def place(
    self, document: Any, directory: Path, stem: str
) -> tuple[Any, list[Path]]:
    """Write each held array to its file and put its pointer in the document.

    Args:
        document: The dumped model, holding marks.
        directory: Where the model's file and its array files go.
        stem: The model file's stem, which every array file name starts with.

    Returns:
        The document with pointers for marks, and the array files written, in
        document order.
    """
    written: list[Path] = []
    if not self.arrays and not self.texts:
        return document, written

    def visit(node: Any, path: tuple[str, ...]) -> Any:
        if isinstance(node, dict):
            if len(node) == 1 and self.mark in node:
                name = ".".join((stem, *map(_file_part, path), "npy"))
                written.append(directory / name)
                return _write(self.arrays[node[self.mark]], directory / name)
            if len(node) == 1 and self.text_mark in node:
                name = ".".join((stem, *map(_file_part, path)))
                written.append(directory / name)
                text = self.texts[node[self.text_mark]]
                return _write_text(text, directory / name)
            return {k: visit(v, (*path, k)) for k, v in node.items()}
        if isinstance(node, list):
            return [visit(v, (*path, str(i))) for i, v in enumerate(node)]
        return node

    return visit(document, ()), written

def serialize_array(value: Any, info: SerializationInfo) -> Any:
    """Dump an array as nested lists, or as a mark when a save puts it in a file."""
    array = np.asarray(value)
    sink = info.context.get(SINK) if isinstance(info.context, dict) else None
    if sink is not None and array.size * 8 > ARRAY_FILE_BYTES:
        return sink.add(array)
    return array.tolist()

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Data is the union of file-only FileData and structured result types. All result types inherit from FileData and require provenance, which identifies the producing program and its optional version. When contained in a ProgramOutput, the concrete type depends on the requested CalcType.

Standalone data objects hold scientific values and producer identity. They do not duplicate the calculation input; retain a ProgramOutput when you need that context.

Empty data is valid for every scientific type. For an empty OptimizationData, final_structure and final_energy return None; structures and energies are empty collections. With frames, a failed final step still contributes its evaluated structure, and any available energy is retained. An unavailable energy is nan, independently of execution success.

docs.title: Frames: structures inside a calculation
docs.text:
A Frame is one structure inside a larger calculation, with what was computed there: an optimizer step, an IRC point, an image of a path. An optimization's frames start with its starting structure, so n steps give n + 1 frames, and final_structure is the last frame's (the optimized one after a success). A frame is a ProgramOutput without input_data (both build on OutputBase: success, logs, traceback, execution). The parent's input already holds the program, model, and keywords, so a frame keeps only its structure and results, a SinglePointData that is never None (empty, with the producing program's provenance, when nothing was computed). ProgramInput.from_spec(parent_spec, frame.structure) rebuilds a step's exact input; Frame.from_output(output) records a subprogram's output as a frame. Passing a ProgramOutput where a frame is expected converts it, taking the step's structure from its input; a saved ProgramOutput is not a frame.

Results that hold frames read the same way: structures, energies (one per frame, nan where none was computed), to_xyz(), and save("x.xyz"), which writes the structures as a multi-structure xyz file. That holds for OptimizationData (one frame per step), PathData, PathOptimizationData (its final path), and ConformerSearchData (its conformers; rotamer_energies reads its rotamers the same way).

PathData is a path of frames in order, with ts_index marking the transition state if there is one. For an IRC the frames run from the end of the reverse branch, through the transition state, to the end of the forward branch; for a chain (NEB, string) they are the images, endpoints included. forward_barrier and reverse_barrier are the transition state's energy above the first and last frames, in Hartree. PathOptimizationData.paths holds the path at every iteration, like an optimization's steps; final_path is the result.

Fields are named after what they hold: frames (OptimizationData, PathData), paths (PathOptimizationData), points (ScanData, one constrained optimization per point), and conformers/rotamers (ConformerSearchData, frames sorted by energy). The former name trajectory (of OptimizationData and ScanData) is not accepted: a payload that uses it fails validation like any unknown field. ConformerSearchData holds frames only; conformer_energies and rotamer_energies are properties that read their energies.

ScanData defaults to no points. Its structures preserves one entry per scan point, using None when a point has no optimization steps. XYZ export raises ValueError if a point lacks a final structure rather than silently omitting it.

Array schemas describe the canonical nested JSON representation: vectors are one-dimensional, geometry/gradients/Hessians are matrices, and normal modes have three dimensions. Constructors continue to accept flat arrays where scientific shape validators can reshape them.

The computed data from a single point calculation.

Attributes:

Name Type Description energy float | None

The electronic energy of the structure in Hartrees.

The gradient of the structure in Hartrees/Bohr.

hessian SerializableMatrix | None

The full Cartesian second derivative of the energy at the input geometry (Eh/bohr^2), 3N x 3N, never projected. Away from a stationary point the gradient gives rotations a part in it, which projection would lose. Projection belongs to vibrational_analysis, which records it.

The nuclear repulsion energy of the structure in Hartrees.

Wavefunction data from the calculation.

The x, y, z components of the dipole moment (e bohr, not Debye) of the method's charge distribution, electrons and nuclei, whatever the method: an SCF density, a force field's or tight-binding model's charges (GFN-FF's EEQ charges), an ML potential's prediction.

3 x 3 quadrupole moment (e bohr^2) of the method's charge distribution, electrons and nuclei, about the coordinate origin, whatever the method: Buckingham's traceless tensor (1/2) sum q (3 r_i r_j - r^2 delta_ij). Programs with another form convert to it.

atomic_charges SerializableVector | None

Partial charge on each atom in units of e, ordered like the structure's atoms. The partitioning scheme (Mulliken, Lowdin, CM5, ...) is the program's; atomic_charges_kind names it.

atomic_charges_kind str | None

The partitioning scheme of atomic_charges: mulliken, lowdin, eeq, eeqbc, cm5, hirshfeld, ...

Alpha minus beta electrons on each atom (e), ordered like the structure's atoms, in the partition atomic_spin_populations_kind names.

atomic_spin_populations_kind str | None

The partitioning scheme of atomic_spin_populations, from the values of atomic_charges_kind; required with them.

atomic_dipoles SerializableMatrix | None

n_atoms x 3: each atom's electronic dipole moment (e bohr) about its own nucleus, mu_A = -sum_{mu on A} (P D^A)_mu,mu with P = P_a + P_b and D^A_nu,mu = , the integrals about the atom of the column AO. Electrons only: no nuclear charge. atomic_quadrupoles SerializableTensor3D | None

n_atoms x 3 x 3: each atom's electronic quadrupole moment (e bohr^2) about its own nucleus, in Buckingham's traceless form (3/2) M - (1/2) tr(M) I, with M_ij = -sum_{mu on A} (P Q^A_ij)_mu,mu and Q^A_ij the integrals of (r - R_A)_i (r - R_A)_j, as for atomic_dipoles.

shell_populations SerializableVector | None

Electrons in each shell of the basis set, sum_{mu in shell} (P S)_mu,mu with P = P_a + P_b, indexed like wavefunction.basis.shells. Populations, not charges, which depend on method-specific reference occupations.

shell_atoms list[int] | None

The atom (0-based) of each shell of shell_populations, so they stand without a basis set; required with them.

shell_angular_momenta list[int] | None

The angular momentum l of each shell of shell_populations; required with them.

point_charge_gradient SerializableMatrix | None

n_charges x 3 gradient of the energy with respect to the positions of external point charges, in Hartrees/Bohr, ordered like the point charges given to the calculation (QM/MM electrostatic embedding).

energy_components dict[str, float]

Terms of the energy (Hartrees) that add up to energy: a partition, never overlapping terms. Standard keys are listed in the conventions (nuclear_repulsion, one_electron, coulomb, exchange, xc, vv10, dispersion, solvation_electrostatic, solvation_cds, ...); what a component contains is the program's (a tight-binding electronic term is not a DFT one). A hierarchy of sub-terms, if a program has one, belongs in the output's record.

Number of SCF iterations of the final SCF.

Expectation value of S^2 of the SCF reference (dimensionless); S(S+1) for a pure spin state, so the excess is the spin contamination.

3 x 3 static dipole polarizability (e^2 bohr^2 / Hartree).

mayer (sum (PS)_mn (PS)_nm over the AOs of two atoms, what xtb prints as "Wiberg"), wiberg (in an orthogonalized basis), ...

The harmonic analysis of the Hessian with the choices behind it (masses, projection, symmetry), when the program made one: the home of frequencies and normal modes.

docs.title: Execution information
docs.text:
Every ProgramOutput has execution: ExecutionInfo, defaulting to an empty ExecutionInfo(). Individual fields may be unknown; explicit execution=None is invalid. Passing ExecutionInfo() or execution={} means output.execution.wall_time returns None without requiring a check for the execution object itself.

host_cpu counts logical CPUs; host_mem_gib accepts fractional values. The former hostcpus and hostmem names are no longer accepted.

wall_time is measured in seconds and host_mem_gib in GiB. host_cpu and host_mem_gib describe host capacity, not the resources allocated to the job. Each frame or scan point records its own execution information, including its working directory.

identities says which code made the results (each program's numerics identity, set by the runner), and store_run names the stored run an output is ("<key>/<run>"): set on every output a store returns and on one a runner has just stored, None on an output no store holds.

Runtime information about a program execution.

All fields may be unknown. Pass ExecutionInfo() when no details are available.

The working directory used by the program.

Elapsed execution time in seconds.

The names of the GPUs the calculation ran on, in device order.

The C library and its version (glibc 2.39). With the CPU and the devices it is the run's environment: results agree across environments to the program's stated round-off, and bitwise only within one.

timings dict[str, float]

Wall-clock seconds per phase of the calculation. The keys are the program's; total is the whole call, and a program with subprograms reports subprograms (time inside them) beside its own phases. An output of a batch also has batch, the whole batch's wall time, set by the runner.

def add_file(self, filepath: Path | str, relative_dir: Path | None = None) -> None:
    """Add a file to the object.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Data structures for specifying quantum chemistry calculations. The most commonly used structure is a ProgramInput which defines a single calculation.

The hierarchy is Files → FileInput → ProgramSpec → ProgramInput. Every input requires program, the requested executor; ProgramOutput.results.provenance.program records the program that actually produced the result.

ProgramSpec describes a calculation without structures. It has its own program, calctype, optional model, keywords, files, cmdline_args, extras, and recursive subprograms. Model remains a distinct scientific concept with method and basis. A program without a meaningful model, such as an optimizer, can leave model=None.

from qcdata import CalcType, ProgramInput, ProgramSpec, Structure

input_data = ProgramInput(
    program="geometric",
    calctype="optimization",
    structure=Structure.open("structure.xyz"),
    keywords={"maxiter": 250},
    subprograms=[
        ProgramSpec(
            program="terachem",
            calctype="gradient",
            model={"method": "wb97x-d3", "basis": "def2-svp"},
            keywords={"convthre": 1e-6},
        ),
    ],
)
gradient_spec = input_data.get_subprogram(CalcType.gradient)

Children can contain further subprograms to arbitrary depth. Each immediate child must have a unique CalcType among its siblings. get_subprogram(calctype) accepts a CalcType or its string value (for example, CalcType.gradient or "gradient"), searches immediate children only, and raises ValueError if missing.

Inputs is FileInput | ProgramInput. Use ProgramInput directly for structured inputs. A ProgramSpec alone is not a top-level input because it lacks structures. Use structure for the constructor argument and attribute; the former molecule API has been removed.

This replaces ProgramArgs, ProgramArgsSub, and DualProgramInput without compatibility aliases. Migrate subprogram and subprogram_args to a subprograms list with an explicit program and calctype on each child. Existing serialized inputs also need these fields. QCSchema AtomicInput conversion requires a non-None model and raises ValueError otherwise.

ProgramInput.structure is the primary/start/reference structure for the calculation. Calculations that require additional complete structures can provide them by role name with ProgramInput.structures, for example structures={"environment": mm_region}. A role may also hold an ordered list of structures. Calculation-specific tools should validate which structure names are required.

A path optimization (calctype="path_optimization": NEB, string, growing string) is about a chain rather than one structure. Its structures, endpoints included and in order, go in structures["initial_chain"], and structure is left out:

ProgramInput(
    program="...",
    calctype="path_optimization",
    structures={"initial_chain": [reactant, *images, product]},  # or [reactant, product]
)

Validation enforces this by calculation type: a path optimization needs a chain of at least two structures with the same atoms and no structure; every other calculation type requires structure. Code that needs one structure calls inp.require_structure(), which returns a Structure (or raises for a chain input) so type checkers know it is not None; inp.initial_chain returns the chain. To restart from a previous path, pass structures={"initial_chain": output.results.final_path.structures}.

FileInput.from_directory("inputs", program="psi4") collects native input files with the required executor identity.

A FileInput is an escape hatch that allows you to run any calculation in any QC program (or any program for that matter), even if it isn't a supported CalcType in qcdata yet. You can use a FileInput to store the native input files (text and binary) for a QC program along with the relevant command line args. Using qcop you can submit a FileInput to a QC program and all output files and logs produced by that program will be collected and returned in a user-friendly ProgramOutput object. FileInput allows you to continue to use qcdata even for calculations that haven't yet been standardized.

docs.title: qcdata.ProgramInput
docs.text:
A program specification bound to structures.

Most calculations are about one structure, structure. A path optimization is about a chain: its structures, endpoints included and in order, go in structures["initial_chain"] and structure is left out. Validation enforces this by calculation type, so structure is always set for every other one; use require_structure() where a type checker needs to know that.

Make a variant by validating changed values, ProgramInput.model_validate(inp.model_dump() | {"calctype": "hessian"}), or at a new geometry with from_spec. Pydantic's model_copy(update=...) does not validate: it would leave calctype a plain string.

Attributes:

Name Type Description structure Structure | None

The primary/start/reference structure; None only for chain calculation types (path_optimization).

structures dict[str, Structure | list[Structure]]

Additional complete structures identified by role, such as a QM/MM environment, or a list of structures for a role that holds several in order, such as "initial_chain".

given SinglePointData | None

Results already known at structure, for the program to start from: an optimizer or IRC takes a given Hessian as its starting Hessian; an SCF starts from a given wavefunction. Starting points, never results: a program does not report a given value as its own. A record of what is known, not a request: a program uses the fields it can, records each one used in its resolved settings ("given"), and leaves the rest alone, so given=frame.results works as it stands. It refuses the input (not_applicable) when it can use none of the fields, or when a field it would use does not fit (another basis). provenance names only the producing program and version; checking the model is the caller's, which knows the producing input. Part of the input, so part of a stored calculation's key.

Example 
from qcdata import ProgramInput, ProgramSpec, Structure

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="geometric",
    calctype="optimization",
    structure=Structure.open("structure.xyz"),
    keywords={"maxiter": 250},
    subprograms=[
        ProgramSpec(
            program="terachem",
            calctype="gradient",
            model={"method": "wb97x-d3", "basis": "def2-svp"},
        ),
    ],
)

def add_files(

    directory: StrOrPath,
    recursive: bool = False,
    exclude: list[str] | None = None,
) -> None:

        recursive: Whether to recursively add files from subdirectories.
        exclude: A list of filenames to exclude from the directory.

    directory = Path(directory)
    if exclude is None:
        exclude = []
    if recursive:
        files = directory.rglob("*")
    else:

def save_files(self, directory: StrOrPath = Path(".")) -> None:
    """Write all files to the specified directory.

    Text data is written in text mode and binary data in binary mode. Parent
    directories are created for filenames that contain relative paths.

    Args:
        directory: The directory to write the files to. Created if it does not
            exist (its parent must already exist). Defaults to the current
            working directory.
    """
    directory = Path(directory)
    directory.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for filename, data in self.files.items():
        mode = "w" if isinstance(data, str) else "wb"
        filepath = directory / filename
        # In case filename is a relative path, create the parent directories
        filepath.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)
        filepath.open(mode).write(data)

Return the key under which a store files the calculation inp requests.

The key is "k1:" and the sha256 hex digest of the canonical JSON form of the input as given. It names the calculation only: which code produced a stored result (each program's numerics identity) is recorded with each run by the runner and the store, not hashed into the key. The canonical form has:

  • keys sorted;
  • numbers normalized: an integral float is written as an integer (100.0 as 100, -0.0 as 0), any other float in its shortest round-trip form;
  • fields at their default left out, so adding a field to qcdata never changes an old key;
  • coordinates in bohr rounded to 1e-10 and written as integers, atom order kept;
  • every other array field (a given Hessian, orbital coefficients) as {"array": shape, "dtype": dtype, "sha256": digest}, the digest of its C-order little-endian bytes: float64 with -0.0 as 0.0, integers in their own dtype. Arrays inside free-form values such as keywords stay JSON numbers;
  • attached files by the sha256 of their bytes (UTF-8 for text);
  • subprograms canonicalized the same way, in order.

Left out: extras at every level, structure identifiers, and the resource keywords threads, memory_gib and device_memory_gib at the top level of keywords, in the input and in every subprogram. Everything else counts, given and backend included. Spellings are not normalized: a synonym or a default written out explicitly gives another key.

def calculation_key(inp: FileInput | ProgramInput) -> str:
    """Return the key under which a store files the calculation ``inp`` requests.

    The key is ``"k1:"`` and the sha256 hex digest of the canonical JSON form of the
    input as given. It names the calculation only: which code produced a stored result
    (each program's numerics identity) is recorded with each run by the runner and the
    store, not hashed into the key. The canonical form has:

    - keys sorted;
    - numbers normalized: an integral float is written as an integer (``100.0`` as
      ``100``, ``-0.0`` as ``0``), any other float in its shortest round-trip form;
    - fields at their default left out, so adding a field to qcdata never changes an
      old key;
    - coordinates in bohr rounded to 1e-10 and written as integers, atom order kept;
    - every other array field (a `given` Hessian, orbital coefficients) as
      ``{"array": shape, "dtype": dtype, "sha256": digest}``, the digest of its C-order
      little-endian bytes: float64 with ``-0.0`` as ``0.0``, integers in their own
      dtype. Arrays inside free-form values such as ``keywords`` stay JSON numbers;
    - attached files by the sha256 of their bytes (UTF-8 for text);
    - subprograms canonicalized the same way, in order.

    Left out: ``extras`` at every level, structure identifiers, and the resource
    keywords ``threads``, ``memory_gib`` and ``device_memory_gib`` at the top level of
    ``keywords``, in the input and in every subprogram. Everything else counts,
    ``given`` and ``backend`` included. Spellings are not normalized: a synonym or a
    default written out explicitly gives another key.

    Args:
        inp: The input as given. A bare `ProgramSpec` is not a calculation; bind it to
            a structure with `ProgramInput.from_spec` first.

    Returns:
        The key, ``"k1:"`` followed by 64 hex digits.

    Raises:
        TypeError: ``inp`` is not an input, or it holds a value JSON cannot represent
            (a set, bytes outside ``files``, a mapping with non-string keys).
        ValueError: The input holds a non-finite number.
    """
    if not isinstance(inp, FileInput) or (
        isinstance(inp, ProgramSpec) and not isinstance(inp, ProgramInput)
    ):
        raise TypeError(
            "A calculation key needs a ProgramInput or a FileInput, not "
            f"{type(inp).__name__}; bind a ProgramSpec with ProgramInput.from_spec."
        )
    text = json.dumps(
        _canonical_model(inp),
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=True,
        allow_nan=False,
    )
    return f"{_VERSION}:{hashlib.sha256(text.encode('ascii')).hexdigest()}"

docs.title: Basis sets and orbitals
docs.text: Wavefunction.orbitals is the one home of a calculation's orbital levels: energies and occupations per spin, the electronic temperature and Fermi levels, and the electrons each atom keeps outside the orbitals (core_electrons). On request it also holds the coefficients, so they can seed another program's SCF, be plotted, or be compared across programs. Wavefunction adds the AO matrices (overlap, hamiltonian_a/_b and core_hamiltonian) and basis, the basis set that the coefficients and every AO matrix share, with the AO convention they follow and its effective core potentials (Ecp). The design and its reasons are in Wavefunctions.

docs.title: qcdata.Wavefunction
docs.text:
The wavefunction of a single point calculation: its orbitals and AO matrices.

The SCF density is not stored: it is C n C^T of the returned orbitals (Orbitals.density). The orbitals' coefficients and the AO matrices come only on request, and all of them are indexed by the AOs of one basis set, basis: it is present whenever any of them is, and only then. An overlap alone therefore ships the basis set and no coefficients. with_convention converts the coefficients and every matrix together.

Attributes:

Name Type Description orbitals Orbitals

The orbital levels and, on request, the orbitals' coefficients.

basis BasisSet | None

The basis set that the coefficients and every AO matrix share (its centers refer to the structure's atoms), in AO order and with its AOConvention; present whenever coefficients or an AO matrix are.

overlap SerializableMatrix | None

The AO overlap matrix S the program used, with its own screening.

hamiltonian_a SerializableMatrix | None

The Fock or Kohn-Sham matrix, or the tight-binding Hamiltonian (Eh), of alpha electrons or of both spins for restricted orbitals: the operator of one build at the SCF's last input (a density, or charges and multipole moments), however that input was mixed. The canonical orbitals are its fresh generalized eigenvectors with the returned S, H C = S C diag(energies). It is built from the last input, not from the returned orbitals' density, which is one step ahead; the two differ by the SCF residual. It holds everything in the SCF operator (exchange-correlation on the final grid, nonlocal correlation, a continuum solvent's operator) and nothing that does not depend on the density (dispersion, a solvent's CDS term). Requesting it changes no other number.

hamiltonian_b SerializableMatrix | None

The beta Hamiltonian (Eh) of unrestricted orbitals.

core_hamiltonian SerializableMatrix | None

Every density-independent one-electron term of the run (Eh): the kinetic energy, the attraction of nuclei with charges Z - core_electrons, the ECPs, and external point charges and fields where a program supports them. tr((P_a + P_b) h), with P the density of the SCF's last input, is the energy's one_electron component; with Orbitals.density, the density a reader has, the two agree to the SCF residual, so compare them at SCF tolerance, not at round-off.

def with_convention(self, convention: AOConvention) -> Wavefunction:
    """The same wavefunction with its AOs in another convention.

    Each array changes with its variance (`BasisSet.transform`): coefficients scale
    by s per AO index and the AO matrices, all operators, by 1 / (s_mu s_nu). The
    orbital levels are shared, not copied.

    Args:
        convention: The target AO convention.

    Returns:
        A new wavefunction whose basis set has the target convention.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the wavefunction has no basis set (only orbital levels).
    """
    basis = self.basis
    if basis is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "with_convention() needs the basis set, and this wavefunction has only "
            "orbital levels: programs return the basis set with the coefficients or "
            "an AO matrix, on request"
        )
    update: dict[str, Any] = {
        "basis": basis.model_copy(update={"ao_convention": convention})
    }
    orbitals = self.orbitals
    coefficients = {
        name: basis.transform(c, convention, kind="coefficients")
        for name in ("coefficients_a", "coefficients_b")
        if (c := getattr(orbitals, name)) is not None
    }
    if coefficients:
        update["orbitals"] = orbitals.model_copy(update=coefficients)
    for name in _AO_MATRICES:
        matrix = getattr(self, name)
        if matrix is not None:
            update[name] = basis.transform(matrix, convention, kind="operator")
    return self.model_copy(update=update)

def density(self) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """The alpha and beta AO density matrices, C n C^T per spin.

    Returns:
        Two nao x nao matrices in the AOs of the wavefunction's basis set.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the orbitals have no coefficients.
    """
    ca = self.coefficients_a
    if ca is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "density() needs the orbitals' coefficients, and these orbitals have "
            "only their levels: programs return coefficients on request (output "
            "orbitals)"
        )
    cb = self.coefficients_b if self.coefficients_b is not None else ca
    return (ca * self.occupations_a) @ ca.T, (cb * self.occupations_b) @ cb.T

def ao_labels(self, symbols: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    """One label per AO, e.g. ``"0 O 2p x"`` or ``"1 H 1s"``.

    Spherical functions are labelled ``d-2 .. d+2``, Cartesian ones ``dxy``; shells
    are numbered by l per atom.

    Args:
        symbols: Element symbols of the structure's atoms, to include in the labels.

    Returns:
        One label per AO, in AO order.
    """
    labels: list[str] = []
    count: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for s in self.shells:
        l = s.angular_momentum
        n = count[(s.center, l)] = count.get((s.center, l), 0) + 1
        atom = (
            f"{s.center} {symbols[s.center]}"
            if symbols is not None
            else f"{s.center}"
        )
        for key in _function_keys(s, self.ao_convention):
            labels.append(f"{atom} {n + l}{_function_name(l, key)}")
    return labels

def transform(
    self,
    array: Any,
    convention: AOConvention,
    *,
    kind: AOArrayKind,
    shell_order: Sequence[int] | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Convert an AO-indexed array to another AO convention and shell order.

    A target AO is a source AO divided by s, the ratio of the function's norm in
    this convention to its norm in the target (1 for every spherical function and
    for a reordering alone). Coefficients therefore scale by s per AO index,
    densities by s_mu s_nu and operators by 1 / (s_mu s_nu); a reordering permutes
    the AO indices of all three alike.

    Args:
        array: The array in this basis set's convention.
        convention: The target convention.
        kind: How the array transforms: ``coefficients`` (its first index is an AO,
            e.g. MO coefficients, nao x nmo), ``operator`` (an nao x nao matrix of
            integrals <mu|O|nu>: overlap, Hamiltonians) or ``density`` (an
            nao x nao matrix that contracts with operators, e.g. C n C^T).
        shell_order: The shells' order in the target, as indices into `shells`;
            None keeps the order.

    Returns:
        A new array in the target convention.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `kind` is unknown or the array does not match the basis set's
            AOs.
    """
    if kind not in ("coefficients", "operator", "density"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"kind must be coefficients, operator or density, not {kind!r}"
        )
    a = np.asarray(array, dtype=float)
    nao = self.nao
    perm, scale = _ao_map(self, convention, shell_order)
    if kind == "coefficients":
        if a.ndim == 0 or a.shape[0] != nao:
            raise ValueError(f"expected {nao} rows (AOs), got shape {a.shape}")
        return a[perm] * scale.reshape((-1,) + (1,) * (a.ndim - 1))
    if a.shape != (nao, nao):
        raise ValueError(f"expected an {nao} x {nao} matrix, got shape {a.shape}")
    moved = a[np.ix_(perm, perm)]
    pair = np.outer(scale, scale)
    return moved / pair if kind == "operator" else moved * pair

The scalar effective core potential of one atom.

The potential is U_L(r) + sum_{l<L} (U_l(r) - U_L(r)) P_l, with P_l the projector on angular momentum l about the atom and L = len(semilocal): the layout of Basis Set Exchange, NWChem, PySCF and Psi4. Spin-orbit terms have no place here. With the number of core electrons it replaces, an ECP is a complete potential; in a Wavefunction, the atom's Orbitals.core_electrons agrees with it.

Attributes:

Name Type Description center int

Index of the atom (0-based) in the structure the basis set belongs to.

core_electrons int

The number of core electrons the potential replaces, so the nucleus enters with charge Z - core_electrons.

local list[EcpTerm]

The terms of U_L, felt by every angular momentum.

semilocal list[list[EcpTerm]]

semilocal[l], for l = 0..L-1: the terms of U_l - U_L.

docs.title: qcdata.AOConvention
docs.text:
How the functions of each shell are ordered and normalized.

Shells are always in the order of BasisSet.shells; this says which functions a shell contributes and in what order. The default is PySCF's ordering with x^l-normalized Cartesian components (libcint). Real solid harmonics are the usual unit-normalized ones without a Condon-Shortley phase (as PySCF, libint and Molden).

Attributes:

Name Type Description spherical_order SphericalOrder

Order of the functions of pure shells.

cartesian_order CartesianOrder

Order of the components of Cartesian shells.

cartesian_normalization CartesianNormalization

Norm of the components of Cartesian shells.

docs.title: qcdata.SphericalOrder
docs.text:
Order of the 2l+1 real solid harmonics of a pure shell.

Attributes:

Name Type Description pyscf

m = -l..l, except p shells, which are (x, y, z) (libcint, PySCF).

increasing_m

m = -l..l for every l, so p is (y, z, x) (libint's "standard", CCA, order).

molden

m = 0, +1, -1, +2, -2, ..., with p as (x, y, z) (Molden, Gaussian, ORCA's order; ORCA also flips the sign of some f and g functions, not covered here).

trexio

m = 0, +1, -1, +2, -2, ... for every l, so p is (z, x, y) (TREXIO).

docs.title: qcdata.CartesianOrder
docs.text:
Order of the (l+1)(l+2)/2 components of a Cartesian shell.

Attributes:

Name Type Description lexicographic

xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz (lx descending, then ly descending; libint, libcint, PySCF, CCA, TREXIO).

molden

xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz; xxx, yyy, zzz, xyy, xxy, xxz, xzz, yzz, yyz, xyz; and Molden's g order (up to l = 4).

docs.title: qcdata.CartesianNormalization
docs.text:
Norm of the components of a Cartesian shell (pure functions always have unit norm).

Attributes:

Name Type Description axis

every component carries the normalization of x^l: x^l, y^l, z^l have unit norm, xy has norm 1/sqrt(3) (libint).

unit

every component has unit norm (Molden).

pyscf

as axis times sqrt(4 pi / (2l + 1)) for l >= 2 (PySCF's cart=True).

docs.title: Outcome: resolved settings, warnings, errors
docs.text: Every output says what the calculation decided and, if it failed, why, in the same fields whichever program produced it. warnings, error and record are on ProgramOutput and on each Frame; resolved only on ProgramOutput. The vocabularies are in Conventions.

docs.title: qcdata.Resolved
docs.text:
The settings a calculation actually used.

Attributes:

Name Type Description settings FreeDict

The program's complete settings tree with every "auto" replaced, in the shape of ProgramInput.keywords. Passed back as keywords, it reproduces the run. Memory- and backend-dependent choices that can change numbers (DF storage, precision per card class) appear here resolved.

Why each automatic choice was made, keyed by dotted settings path ("grid.xc": "calctype hessian: a finer grid").

In a plan only: dotted paths of settings left "auto" because the run decides them ("jk.df_storage" from the free memory when the SCF starts). A finished output's resolved settings have every "auto" replaced and nothing deferred.

docs.title: qcdata.ErrorInfo
docs.text:
A structured description of a failure.

The Python traceback stays in ProgramOutput.traceback; this is what a caller branches on.

Attributes:

Name Type Description kind ErrorKind

The kind of failure.

message str

A human-readable explanation.

code str | None

A stable snake_case code that refines kind: one the conventions share (scf_not_converged, host_memory) or one the program defines and documents (max_iter, energy_rose, not_first_order_saddle). Callers branch on it instead of parsing message.

The subprogram that failed (kind program), or the program that failed when it is not the top-level one.

The subprogram's own error, for kind program: "the gradient failed because the SCF did not converge" stays structured through every level.

Structured facts about the failure, as plain JSON, so callers need not parse message. The conventions name the keys of shared codes: required_gib and available_gib for host_memory and device_memory, when the program knows them, in the memory keyword's terms: the memory_gib (device_memory_gib) with which the calculation would fit, and the one it ran with (GiB).

docs.title: qcdata.ErrorKind
docs.text:
Why a calculation failed, in one vocabulary across programs.

Attributes:

Name Type Description input

Settings or a structure the program cannot run as given (an unknown key, a bad value, an unknown basis set or method).

unsupported

A valid request the program does not implement, or a setting it cannot honour that would change the result.

convergence

An iterative procedure (SCF, response equations, an optimization) did not converge; the results reached are attached.

numerical

A numerical failure: non-finite values, singular matrices.

resource

Not enough memory, disk, or another resource as set up.

backend

The hardware backend failed (no usable GPU, a device error).

program

A subprogram failed; ErrorInfo.cause holds its error.

timeout

The calculation ran out of time (set by the runner).

stopped

The program stopped on request at one of its steps (a runner's stop, which the program sees as ctx.stop_requested()); the partial output it reached is attached. Not a fault of the calculation, so a runner never stores a stopped output and a store never reuses one.

environment

The program could not be run at all: not installed, no licence, the process died (set by the runner).

internal

A failure nobody anticipated: a bug (an exception other than ProgramError, a broken invariant, a crash), or a failure no rule classifies (an unexplained exit, unreadable output). A failure a program anticipates takes the kind that fits it.
