@classmethod
def failure(
    cls,
    input_data: ProgramInputType,
    error: ErrorInfo,
    *,
    results: Any = None,
    traceback: str | None = None,
    **fields: Any,
) -> ProgramOutput[ProgramInputType, Any]:
    """A failed output of the right shape for its input's calculation type.

    Programs return this instead of building empty results by hand: an
    ``optimization`` input needs `OptimizationData` results even when nothing ran.

    Args:
        input_data: The input that failed.
        error: Why it failed.
        results: Partial results, if any; else empty results of the calctype's
            data type with the program's provenance.
        traceback: The failure's details; defaults to the error's message.
        **fields: Other output fields (``logs``, ``execution``, ``warnings``,
            ``record``).

    Returns:
        The failed output.
    """
    from .base_models import Provenance
    from .data import get_data_type
    from .inputs import ProgramInput as _ProgramInput

    if results is None:
        data_type = (
            get_data_type(input_data.calctype)
            if isinstance(input_data, _ProgramInput)
            else FileData
        )
        results = data_type(provenance=Provenance(program=input_data.program))
    return ProgramOutput(
        input_data=input_data,
        results=results,
        success=False,
        error=error,
        traceback=traceback or error.message,
        **fields,
    )

docs.title: Canonical results field
docs.text:
Scientific models retain their Data names and can exist independently of an execution. Within ProgramOutput, that data is the calculation's results: use output.results.energy, output.results.gradient, or output.results.final_structure.

The results live in "results". The former name "data" is not accepted: a payload that uses it fails validation like any unknown field, and the .data attribute is gone.

The old Results and *Results classes, qcdata.models.results module, qcio import shim, stdout/files forwarding, and deprecated convenience helpers have been removed. Use ProgramOutput, *Data, logs, results.files, and explicit scientific attributes instead.

docs.title: Input and result contract
docs.text:
The result type depends on the input, regardless of success or failure:

Input Result type FileInput FileData only Energy, gradient, Hessian ProgramInput SinglePointData Optimization or transition-state ProgramInput OptimizationData Conformer-search ProgramInput ConformerSearchData Scan ProgramInput ScanData IRC ProgramInput PathData Path-optimization ProgramInput PathOptimizationData

Successful single-point calculations require the requested value; successful optimizations and IRCs require frames, scans require points, path optimizations require paths, and successful conformer searches require conformers. Failed calculations require a traceback and retain the corresponding scientific type, with empty or partial values allowed. Producer provenance is always required.

When deserializing, ProgramOutput uses the input contract to select the result model. Empty scientific payloads therefore retain their type when saved and reopened, including inside frames and scan points. No additional serialized type tag is needed. Explicit generic types must agree with the input contract.

input_data belongs on ProgramOutput, not inside results. Save the whole output when you need scientific values together with the requested calculation and execution context. Save a standalone data object when exchanging only scientific values and producer identity.

docs.title: Migrating existing outputs
docs.text:
This is a breaking schema change with no automatic legacy-provenance loader:

  • Move provenance.program, provenance.program_version, and provenance.extras into results.provenance.
  • Move scratch_dir, wall_time, and hostname into execution; rename hostcpus to host_cpu and hostmem to host_mem_gib. Memory accepts fractional GiB. These renames have no compatibility aliases.
  • Remove the old top-level provenance field.
  • Use FileData(provenance=...) only with FileInput. For failed structured calculations, construct the corresponding scientific type, such as SinglePointData(provenance=...), and update generic annotations accordingly.
  • Apply the same migration to each nested trajectory output. Do not copy parent provenance or execution information to children.

Standalone structured data now also requires explicit provenance.

External callers must migrate too: qccodec should attach the parsed producer and version to the returned data; qccompute should supply execution and return the corresponding scientific data type even when a structured calculation fails without producing values.

docs.title: Reconstructed frames
docs.text: Parsers reconstruct frames from what a program saved (structures and energies, sometimes gradients). Such frames describe recovered scientific evaluations, which need not be separate process invocations, and carry no input of their own: the parent output's input describes the calculation. A frame's results holds whatever was recovered; missing an optional gradient does not by itself make a frame a failure.

docs.title: 🧠 qcdata operates on a simple mental model
docs.text:
• Structure objects represent a collection of atoms, a molecule, or any super molecular structure in 3D cartesian space.
  • Input objects define the parameters for a calculation.
  • ProgramOutput objects store computed values and output files, while Data objects represent the structured result payload for a calculation. ProgramOutput also stores the exact input data (.input_data) used for a calculation, logs and ExecutionInfo. Each data payload holds its own Provenance so you have full visibility into how every result was generated.
  • Other objects, such as Identifiers, Files, Provenance, and Model support these core data structures by organizing relevant information in a user-friendly way.
  • 💾 Saving your data to disk and re-opening it again later for analysis is as simple as calling my_obj.save(/path/to/file.json) or MyModel.open(/path/to/file.json). These methods are not shown in the documentation for individual classes to avoid redundancy. Files can be saved as .json, .yaml, or .toml. Structure and OptimizationData (which contains a list of Structures) may additionally be saved as .xyz files for compatibility with external program.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
Provenance identifies the program that produced a result. It belongs on FileData and every structured result type, accessed as output.results.provenance. Saving data independently preserves this identity.

program is required; program_version is optional. Provenance is also required for manually constructed data and empty failure payloads. Callers must supply the program identity explicitly; qcdata does not infer it from input_data.program.

Each frame has its own data provenance. For example, optimization data can identify geomeTRIC while gradient data identifies TeraChem. Runtime details belong in ExecutionInfo.

For empty failure results, program identifies the intended scientific producer even if execution never began. Its version remains None unless known. The output's success, traceback, and execution metadata describe what actually happened.

docs.title: Base model behavior
docs.text:
All qcdata models have a read-only qcdata_version property holding the installed package version. A dumped object is a document: model_dump(), model_dump_json(), save() and json_dumps() write qcdata_version at its top level only, even with exclude_unset=True (pass exclude={"qcdata_version"} to leave it out), and nested objects carry none. extras is left out wherever it is empty. Neither appears in the usual representation, to keep scientific values readable.

On loading, a saved stamp is accepted and discarded; serialization supplies the current version. This identifies the last writer of the representation, not the original creator, a minimum reader version, or a formal schema version. Reading a stamped file does not guarantee that an older or newer package can interpret it. Files without a stamp are accepted normally.

JSON, YAML, and TOML preserve this metadata. Structure XYZ exports include it as a comment token. External QCSchema conversions exclude it from model and identifier fields.

docs.title: Mutation and persistence
docs.text:
Attribute assignment is frozen, but nested dictionaries, lists, and arrays are not deeply immutable. Direct container mutation is unsupported. Use model_dump(), edit the returned built-in values, and reconstruct with model_validate() so validation runs again. Scientific array fields dump as independent lists. Arbitrary custom objects in extras are not covered by this independence guarantee. File-collection helpers and Structure.add_identifiers() remain explicit mutation exceptions.

save() returns every file it wrote, the model's file first. An array field whose float64 size exceeds 1 MiB is written to its own .npy file beside the saved file, named by the file's stem and the array's path (output.results.hessian.npy), and the document holds a pointer with its relative path, shape, dtype and sha256; open() reads it back, so models always hold arrays. Smaller arrays stay in the document and round-trip exactly through JSON and YAML. See Saved files.

save() is lossless by default (exclude_unset=False), so containers filled after construction are kept. Pass exclude_unset=True for a compact file without the fields omitted during construction; explicitly supplied values are retained even when equal to their defaults, and the version stamp is still written. exclude_none=True remains the default.

Supported file and identifier helpers mark changed fields as set so those changes are saved. Direct mutation of initially unset containers is unsupported and may be omitted. The dump/edit/validate workflow preserves edits, but reconstructing from a full dump makes its fields explicitly set and can produce larger files.

@classmethod
def open(cls, filepath: Path | str) -> Self:
    """Instantiate an object from data saved to disk.

    Arrays that `save` put in their own `.npy` files are read back from beside the
    file, each checked against the sha256, shape and dtype saved with it.

    Args:
        filepath: The path to the object on disk.

    Returns:
        The instantiated object.

    Example:
        ```python
        my_obj = MyModel.open("path/to/file.json")
        ```
    """
    filepath = Path(filepath)
    data = filepath.read_text()
    context = {array_files.DIRECTORY: filepath.parent}

    if filepath.suffix in [".yaml", ".yml"]:
        import yaml  # imported on use: most callers never read YAML

        return cls.model_validate(yaml.safe_load(data), context=context)
    elif filepath.suffix == ".toml":
        import toml

        return cls.model_validate(toml.loads(data), context=context)

    # Assume json for all other file extensions
    return cls.model_validate_json(data, context=context)

save(
    filepath: Path | str,
    exclude_none: bool = True,
    exclude_unset: bool = False,
    indent: int = 4,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> list[Path]

Save an object to disk as json, yaml, or toml.

Objects such as Structure and OptimizationData can additionally be saved as xyz files.

Every array field whose float64 size exceeds 1 MiB is written to its own .npy file beside the saved file, named by the file's stem and the array's path in the document (output.results.hessian.npy for output.json). The document holds a pointer in its place: {"path", "shape", "dtype", "sha256"}, the digest being the .npy file's. A text in files over 1 MiB (UTF-8) goes to a file of its own the same way, named by the stem and its path with no suffix added (output.results.files.orbitals%2Emolden), with {"path", "sha256"} in its place. open reads them back, so a model never holds a file reference. These files are written first and the model's file last. Smaller arrays and texts stay in the document, where every float round-trips exactly through JSON and YAML.

Note

By default the object will be saved as a json file. If the file extension is .yaml or .yml, the object will be saved as a yaml file. If the file extension is .toml, the object will be saved as a toml file. If the file extension is .xyz, the object will be saved as an xyz file (for objects that support this format such as a Structure or an OptimizationData whose frames hold structures).

Additionally, padding will be added to the file by default to make it more human-readable. You can adjust the amount of padding added by changing the indent parameter. Pass indent=None to create a more compact file. An indented JSON file keeps each innermost array (a list holding no lists or objects, such as a row of coordinates) on one line.

def save(
    self,
    filepath: Path | str,
    exclude_none: bool = True,
    exclude_unset: bool = False,
    indent: int = 4,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> list[Path]:
    """Save an object to disk as `json`, `yaml`, or `toml`.

    Objects such as `Structure` and `OptimizationData` can additionally be saved
    as `xyz` files.

    Every array field whose float64 size exceeds 1 MiB is written to its own `.npy`
    file beside the saved file, named by the file's stem and the array's path in
    the document (`output.results.hessian.npy` for `output.json`). The document
    holds a pointer in its place: `{"path", "shape", "dtype", "sha256"}`, the
    digest being the `.npy` file's. A text in `files` over 1 MiB (UTF-8) goes to
    a file of its own the same way, named by the stem and its path with no suffix
    added (`output.results.files.orbitals%2Emolden`), with `{"path", "sha256"}` in
    its place. `open` reads them back, so a model never holds a file reference.
    These files are written first and the model's file last. Smaller arrays and
    texts stay in the document, where every float round-trips exactly through
    JSON and YAML.

    Note:
        By default the object will be saved as a `json` file. If the file extension
        is `.yaml` or `.yml`, the object will be saved as a `yaml` file. If the file
        extension is `.toml`, the object will be saved as a `toml` file. If the file
        extension is `.xyz`, the object will be saved as an `xyz` file (for objects
        that support this format such as a `Structure` or an `OptimizationData`
        whose frames hold structures).

        Additionally, padding will be added to the file by default to make it more
        human-readable. You can adjust the amount of padding added by changing the
        `indent` parameter. Pass `indent=None` to create a more compact file. An
        indented JSON file keeps each innermost array (a list holding no lists or
        objects, such as a row of coordinates) on one line.

    Args:
        filepath: The path to write the object to.
        exclude_none: If True, attributes with a value of None will not be written.
            Changing default behavior from pydantic.model_dump() to True.
        exclude_unset: If True, fields omitted during construction are not written,
            even when their containers were filled in later (a `record` a program
            filled after building the output would be lost). Defaults to False, so
            a save is lossless.
        indent: The number of spaces to use for indentation in the JSON file. 0
            creates a more compact JSON file, 4 is more human-readable.
        **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to the serialization method.

    Returns:
        Every file written: the model's file first, then one file per array or text
        saved apart, in document order.

    Example:
        ```python
        my_obj.save("path/to/file.json")
        ```

        ```python
        my_obj.save("path/to/file.yaml")
        ```

        ```python
        my_obj.save("path/to/file.toml")
        ```

        ```python
        my_obj.save("path/to/file.xyz")
        ```
    """
    filepath = Path(filepath)
    filepath.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)

    sink = array_files.ArraySink(text_files=True)
    model_dict = self.model_dump(
        mode="json",
        exclude_none=exclude_none,
        exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
        context={array_files.SINK: sink},
        **kwargs,
    )
    model_dict, array_paths = sink.place(model_dict, filepath.parent, filepath.stem)

    if filepath.suffix in [".yaml", ".yml"]:
        import yaml

        data = yaml.dump(model_dict, indent=indent)

    elif filepath.suffix == ".toml":
        import toml

        data = toml.dumps(model_dict)

    elif indent is None:
        data = json.dumps(model_dict)
    else:
        # Write data to json regardless of file extension
        data = _indented_json(model_dict, indent)

    filepath.write_text(data)
    return [filepath, *array_paths]

docs.title: Session steps: requests, accuracy, failures
docs.text: A session (qccompute's execution protocol) evaluates one molecule at many geometries. What one step asks for and how it fails are data, shared by every program: a Request, its Accuracy target, and ProgramError, the exception form of ErrorInfo. A step's result is a Frame. Lineages are any JSON value; programs key their histories by lineage_key. An input's own target, for compute and for requests that give none, is the shared keyword accuracy (conventions), read with Accuracy.from_keywords.

docs.title: qcdata.Request
docs.text:
One step of a session: where to evaluate, what, and from which history.

Attributes:

Name Type Description positions SerializableMatrix | None

Atomic positions (bohr), n_atoms x 3, atoms as the session's input. None: the input's own geometry.

calctype CalcType | None

energy, gradient or hessian; None: the input's calctype.

accuracy Accuracy | float | None

Target accuracy of this request (a bare number targets the calctype's highest derivative); it replaces the input's accuracy keyword for this request. None: the keyword's target, else the session's settings.

lineage Lineage

The chain of steps this one continues. A session keeps warm-start and extrapolation history per lineage (keyed by lineage_key), so NEB images, IRC branches and parallel tasks each start from their own last success. None is the default lineage.

outputs frozenset[str]

Optional outputs that do not change the surface but may cost extra. A name that fills a top-level SinglePointData field is that field's name (dipole_moment, polarizability); others name what they add (ir). The wavefunction's parts are orbitals, overlap, hamiltonian and core_hamiltonian; a program fills in what one implies (each brings the basis set, hamiltonian also overlap and orbitals), as the conventions list. A program refuses an output it cannot give with kind unsupported, code not_applicable.

seed list[Lineage]

Lineages to start from, in order, when lineage has no history yet: the first with history is used, and with none the request starts fresh. Both IRC branches start from the transition state's lineage this way. A request seeded from a lineage runs after every earlier request of that lineage in the same list. The record names the lineage used.

commit bool

Whether a success becomes lineage's history. False stores nothing: a finite-difference fan-out in the center's lineage starts every displacement from the center, without keeping a state per displacement. In a list, a request reads its lineage's history as it stands at its own place: after every earlier committing request of that lineage, unaffected by later ones. In [A, B (commit=False), C, D (commit=False)], all in one lineage, B starts from A and D from C; B may run alongside C if it reads the history from before C.

docs.title: qcdata.Accuracy
docs.text:
How tightly a calculation converges: targets, absolute and in atomic units.

Each field is the numerical error from convergence the caller can tolerate in that quantity; a field left out sets no target for it. It is a target, not a guarantee: the program picks the thresholds it expects to meet it (a DFT program: SCF orbital gradient and response residual; axtb: energy and charge change) and records the target, the thresholds and any error estimate it has under the shared record key accuracy. Explicit convergence settings are floors: a target may tighten them, never loosen them. Approximations (basis, grids, precision) are not covered.

A target is given two ways. The shared keyword accuracy (an object of these fields, read with from_keywords) is the input's own target: of compute, and of every session request that gives none. A request's Request.accuracy replaces it for that request. The keyword is part of the input, so of its calculation key: a tighter target is another calculation. A program with no convergence settings (a force field, an ML potential) accepts a target, keyword or request alike, and records it as met: empty thresholds and an estimate of 0.0 per target. A program whose convergence settings take no targets yet refuses it with kind unsupported.

Attributes:

Name Type Description energy float | None

Target error of the energy (Eh).

gradient float | None

Target error of the largest absolute gradient component (Eh/bohr).

hessian float | None

Target error of the largest absolute Hessian element (Eh/bohr^2).

@classmethod
def from_keywords(cls, keywords: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Accuracy | None:
    """Read the shared keyword ``accuracy``: the input's own target, if it sets one.

    The keyword is a JSON object of `Accuracy`'s targets
    (``{"energy": 1e-8, "gradient": 1e-6}``), never a bare number: an input's
    target applies to every calctype a session runs, so a number would have no
    single quantity to aim at. An `Accuracy` given in keywords is stored in this
    form (`ProgramSpec.keywords`).

    Args:
        keywords: The input's keywords (`ProgramSpec.keywords`).

    Returns:
        The target, or None when the keywords set none (absent or null).

    Raises:
        ProgramError: Kind ``input``: the value is not an object of positive,
            finite targets; code ``unknown_key`` for a key other than ``energy``,
            ``gradient`` and ``hessian``, and ``no_effect`` when it sets none.
    """
    value = keywords.get("accuracy")
    if value is None:
        return None
    if not isinstance(value, Mapping):
        raise ProgramError.of(
            "input",
            "The keyword accuracy is a JSON object of targets (energy in Eh, "
            "gradient in Eh/bohr, hessian in Eh/bohr^2), such as "
            f'{{"gradient": 1e-06}}, not {type(value).__name__} {value!r}.',
        )
    unknown = sorted(set(value) - set(_TARGETS))
    if unknown:
        import difflib  # imported on use: only a refusal needs it

        hints = [
            f"accuracy.{k}"
            + "".join(
                f" (did you mean accuracy.{m}?)"
                for m in difflib.get_close_matches(k, _TARGETS, n=1)
            )
            for k in unknown
        ]
        raise ProgramError.of(
            "input",
            f"Unknown keyword {', '.join(hints)}; accuracy takes "
            f"{', '.join(_TARGETS)}.",
            code="unknown_key",
        )
    try:
        accuracy = cls.model_validate(value)
    except ValidationError as e:
        errors = "; ".join(
            f"accuracy.{'.'.join(map(str, err['loc']))}: "
            + err["msg"].removeprefix("Value error, ").rstrip(".")
            for err in e.errors()
        )
        raise ProgramError.of(
            "input", f"The keyword accuracy is not valid: {errors}."
        ) from None
    if accuracy.energy is accuracy.gradient is accuracy.hessian is None:
        raise ProgramError.of(
            "input",
            "The keyword accuracy sets no target; give energy, gradient or "
            "hessian, or leave it out.",
            code="no_effect",
        )
    return accuracy

@classmethod
def of(
    cls, value: Accuracy | float | None, calctype: CalcType | str
) -> Accuracy | None:
    """Read a request's accuracy: a bare number targets its highest derivative.

    Args:
        value: An `Accuracy`, a number, or None.
        calctype: The request's calculation type.

    Returns:
        The accuracy, or None when the request gives none: the input's own target
        (`from_keywords`) then applies, else the session's settings.

    if value is None or isinstance(value, Accuracy):
        return value
    name = {"energy": "energy", "gradient": "gradient", "hessian": "hessian"}.get(
        CalcType(calctype).value, "energy"
    )
    return cls.model_validate({name: float(value)})

def __init__(
    self,
    error: ErrorInfo,
    results: Data | None = None,
    *,
    frame: Frame | None = None,
    output: ProgramOutput[Any, Any] | None = None,
):
    """Create the exception.

    Args:
        error: What went wrong.
        results: Partial results, if any; when not given, taken from ``output``,
            else from ``frame``.
        frame: The failed step, if any.
        output: The failed output, if any.
    """
    super().__init__(f"{error.kind}: {error.message}")
    self.error = error
    self.frame = frame
    self.output = output
    if results is None and output is not None:
        results = output.results
    if results is None and frame is not None:
        results = frame.results
    self.results = results

@classmethod
def from_xyz(
    cls,
    xyz_str: str,
    *,
    charge: int | None = None,
    multiplicity: int | None = None,
) -> Self:
    """Create a Structure from an XYZ file or string.

    Args:
        xyz_str: The XYZ string.
        charge: The molecular charge of the structure. If not provided, will read
            from the XYZ string if set or default to 0.
        multiplicity: The molecular multiplicity of the structure. If not provided,
            will read from the XYZ string if set or default to 1.

    Note:
        Will read qcdata data such as `charge` and `multiplicity` from the comments
        line with a `qcdata_key=value` format (if it is present). Also will read in
        qcdata__identifiers_* keys and additional non-qcdata comments.

    Example:
        ```python
        struct = Structure.from_xyz(xyz_str)
        ```
    """
    lines = xyz_str.split("\n")

    num_atoms = int(lines[0])

    # Collect comments
    structure_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {}
    identifier_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {}
    other_comments: list[str] = []

    for item in lines[1].strip().split():
        if item.startswith("qcdata_version="):
            continue  # The current writer's version is supplied on export.
        elif item.startswith("qcdata__identifiers_"):
            key = item.split("=")[0].replace("qcdata__identifiers_", "")
            value = item.split("=")[1]
            identifier_kwargs[key] = value
        elif item.startswith("qcdata_"):
            key = item.split("=")[0].replace("qcdata_", "")
            value = item.split("=")[1]
            structure_kwargs[key] = value
        else:
            other_comments.append(item)

    if charge is not None and "charge" in structure_kwargs:
        raise ValueError("Charge cannot be set in the file and as an argument.")
    if multiplicity is not None and "multiplicity" in structure_kwargs:
        raise ValueError(
            "Multiplicity cannot be set in the file and as an argument."
        )

    # Set charge and multiplicity if provided
    if charge is not None:
        structure_kwargs["charge"] = charge
    if multiplicity is not None:
        structure_kwargs["multiplicity"] = multiplicity

    symbols = []
    geometry = []
    for line in lines[2 : 2 + num_atoms]:
        split_line = line.split()
        symbols.append(split_line[0])
        geometry.append(
            [float(val) / constants.BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM for val in split_line[1:]]
        )

    return cls(
        symbols=symbols,
        geometry=np.asarray(geometry),
        **structure_kwargs,
        identifiers=Identifiers(**identifier_kwargs),
        extras={cls._xyz_comment_key: other_comments},
    )

def to_xyz(self, precision: int = 17) -> str:
    """Return an xyz string representation of the structure.

    Args:
        precision: The number of decimal places to include in the xyz file. Default
            17 which captures all precision of float64.

    Notes:
        Will add qcdata data such as charge and multiplicity to the comments line with
        a `qcdata_key=value` format.
    """
    qcdata_data = {  # These get added to comments line (line 2) in xyz file
        "qcdata_charge": self.charge,
        "qcdata_multiplicity": self.multiplicity,
        "qcdata_version": self.qcdata_version,
    }

    # Add identifiers to qcdata_data
    for key, value in self.identifiers.__dict__.items():
        if key != "extras" and value:
            qcdata_data[f"qcdata__identifiers_{key}"] = value

    assert isinstance(self.geometry, np.ndarray)  # For mypy
    geometry_angstrom = self.geometry * constants.BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM

    xyz_lines = []
    xyz_lines.append(f"{len(self.symbols)}")
    # Add qcdata data to comments line
    comments = f"{' '.join([f'{k}={v}' for k, v in qcdata_data.items()])}"
    # Add any other comments
    if xyz_comments := self.extras.get(self._xyz_comment_key, []):
        comments += " " + " ".join(xyz_comments)
    xyz_lines.append(comments)

    # Create a format string using the precision parameter
    format_str = f"{{:2s}} {{: >18.{precision}f}} {{: >18.{precision}f}} {{: >18.{precision}f}}"  # noqa: E501

    for symbol, (x, y, z) in zip(self.symbols, geometry_angstrom, strict=False):
        xyz_lines.append(format_str.format(symbol, x, y, z))
    xyz_lines.append("")  # Append newline to end of file
    return "\n".join(xyz_lines)

def distance(self, i: int, j: int, units: LengthUnit = LengthUnit.BOHR) -> float:
    """Calculate the distance between two atoms.

    Args:
        i: The index of the first atom.
        j: The index of the second atom.
        units: The units to return the distance in. Defaults to "bohr".
            May be "bohr" or "angstrom".

    Returns:
        The distance between the atoms in units (Bohr or Angstrom).

    Example:
        ```python
        struct.distance(0, 1)
        1.34
        ```
    """
    distance = np.linalg.norm(self.geometry[i] - self.geometry[j])
    if units == LengthUnit.ANGSTROM:
        return float(distance * constants.BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM)
    return float(distance)

def json_dumps(
    obj: BaseModel | list[BaseModel],
    exclude_unset: bool = True,
    indent: int | None = None,
    **model_dump_kwargs: Any,
) -> str:
    """Serialization helper for lists of pydantic objects.

    Args:
        obj: The object to serialize. Either a single pydantic object or a list of pydantic
            objects.
        exclude_unset: Whether to exclude fields omitted during construction.
            Defaults to True for compact output; pass False to include all fields.
        indent: JSON indentation, or None for compact output.
        **model_dump_kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to model_dump.
            Serialization always uses JSON mode.
    """
    mode = model_dump_kwargs.pop("mode", "json")
    if mode != "json":
        raise ValueError("json_dumps requires JSON serialization mode.")

    def dump(model: BaseModel) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return model.model_dump(
            mode="json", exclude_unset=exclude_unset, **model_dump_kwargs
        )

    payload = [dump(model) for model in obj] if isinstance(obj, list) else dump(obj)
    return json.dumps(payload, indent=indent)

def view(
    *objs: ProgramOutput | Frame | Structure | list[Structure],
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> None:
    """Display any qcdata objects in a Jupyter Notebook.

    This is the top-level viewing function and should be the only one needed to view
    any qcdata object.

    Args:
        *objs: The ProgramOutput, Frame, or Structure objects to view. May pass one
            or more objects or one or more lists of Structure objects. A Frame (a
            step of an optimization or a point of a path) shows its structure.
        **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to the viewer functions.

    Returns:
        None. Displays the qcdata objects in the Jupyter Notebook.
    """
    if all([isinstance(o, Structure) for o in objs]) or all(
        isinstance(o, Structure) for lst in objs for o in lst
    ):
        structures(*objs, **kwargs)  # type: ignore
        # Handle all structures in a single viewer
        return

    for obj in objs:
        if isinstance(obj, Structure) or isinstance(obj, list):
            structures(*objs, **kwargs)  # type: ignore

        elif isinstance(obj, ProgramOutput):
            program_outputs(obj, **kwargs)

        elif isinstance(obj, Frame):
            structures(obj.structure, **kwargs)

        else:
            raise NotImplementedError(f"Viewing of {type(obj)} is not implemented.")

def program_outputs(
    *results: ProgramOutput[Inputs, Data],
    animate: bool = True,
    struct_viewer: bool = True,
    conformer_rmsd_threshold: float | None = None,
    conformer_rmsd_backend: str = "rdkit",
    conformer_rmsd_kwargs: dict | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> None:
    """Display one or many ProgramOutput objects.

    Args:
        *results: The ProgramOutput objects to display.
        animate: Whether to animate the structure if it is an optimization.
        struct_viewer: Whether to display the structure viewer.
        conformer_rmsd_threshold: The RMSD threshold in Bohr below which conformers are
            considered duplicates and hidden. If None (default), all conformers are
            shown.
        conformer_rmsd_backend: The qcinf backend used to compute conformer RMSDs
            when filtering. Only used if conformer_rmsd_threshold is set.
        conformer_rmsd_kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to the conformer
            RMSD filtering function.
        **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to the viewer functions.

    Returns:
        None. Displays the ProgramOutput objects in the Jupyter Notebook.
    """
    width = kwargs.get("width", DEFAULT_WIDTH)
    height = kwargs.get("height", DEFAULT_HEIGHT)

    for i, result in enumerate(results):
        final_html = []
        final_html.append(generate_output_table(result))

        if isinstance(result.results, ConformerSearchData) and isinstance(
            result.input_data, ProgramInput
        ):
            structures = [result.input_data.require_structure()]

            if conformer_rmsd_threshold is not None:
                keep_indices = filter_conformers_indices(
                    result.results.structures,
                    backend=conformer_rmsd_backend,
                    threshold=conformer_rmsd_threshold,
                    **(conformer_rmsd_kwargs or {}),
                )
                conformers = [result.results.structures[i] for i in keep_indices]
                energies_rel = result.results.conformer_energies_relative[keep_indices]
            else:
                conformers = result.results.structures
                energies_rel = result.results.conformer_energies_relative

            structures += conformers
            titles_extra = ["Initial Structure"] + [
                f"Conformer {i}" for i in range(len(conformers))
            ]
            subtitles = ["Rel Energy: Unknown"] + [
                "Rel Energy: Unknown"
                if np.isnan(re)
                else f"Rel Energy: +{re * constants.HARTREE_TO_KCAL_PER_MOL:.3f} kcal/mol"
                for re in energies_rel
            ]
            conf_viewer = generate_structure_viewer_html(
                *structures, titles_extra=titles_extra, subtitles=subtitles, **kwargs
            )
            final_html.append(conf_viewer)
            display(HTML("".join(final_html)))

        else:
            # Create structure viewer
            if not struct_viewer:
                structure_html = "struct_viewer = False"
            elif not isinstance(result.input_data, ProgramInput):
                structure_html = "No structure available."
            else:
                titles_extra = kwargs.pop("titles_extra", [])
                try:
                    title_extra = titles_extra[i]
                except IndexError:
                    title_extra = ""

                # Determine the Structure to use
                if isinstance(result.results, OptimizationData):
                    for_viewer: Structure | list[Structure]
                    if not result.results.frames:
                        for_viewer = result.input_data.require_structure()
                        title_extra += " (Initial Structure; no optimization steps)"
                    elif animate:
                        for_viewer = result.results.structures
                    else:
                        for_viewer = result.results.structures[-1]
                        title_extra += " (Last Evaluated Structure)"

                elif isinstance(result.results, (PathData, PathOptimizationData)):
                    path = result.results.structures
                    if not path:
                        for_viewer = (
                            result.input_data.structure
                            or result.input_data.initial_chain
                        )
                        title_extra += " (Input; no path computed)"
                    else:
                        for_viewer = path
                        title_extra += " (Path)"

                elif isinstance(result.results, SinglePointData):
                    for_viewer = result.input_data.require_structure()

                elif isinstance(result.results, FileData):
                    for_viewer = result.input_data.require_structure()
                else:
                    raise NotImplementedError(
                        f"Viewing of {type(result.results)} is not yet implemented."
                    )

                structure_html = generate_structure_viewer_html(
                    for_viewer,
                    titles_extra=[title_extra],
                    **kwargs,
                )

            # Create data table or plot
            if isinstance(result.results, OptimizationData):
                data_html = generate_optimization_plot(
                    result, figsize=(width / 100, height / 100)
                )
            else:
                data_html = generate_data_table(result.results)

            final_html.append(
                f"""
        <div style="text-align: center;">
            <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: 
                space-around;">
                <div style="text-align: center; margin-right: 20px; flex: 1;">
                    <div style="display: inline-block; text-align: center;">
                        {structure_html}
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div style="width: {width}px; height: {height}px; text-align: center; 
                    margin-left: 20px; flex: 1; overflow: auto;">
                    {data_html}
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
                """
            )

            display(HTML("".join(final_html)))

    titles = titles or []
    subtitles = subtitles or []
    titles_extra = titles_extra or []
    subtitles_extra = subtitles_extra or []

    # Start HTML with flex container
    html_parts = [
        '<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: center;">'
    ]

    if not view_2d:
        # Create the viewer
        if len(structs) == 1 or same_viewer:
            viewer = p3d.view(width=width, height=height)
        else:
            # Determine the number of rows needed for multiple structures
            rows = math.ceil(len(structs) / 2)
            viewer = p3d.view(
                width=width * 2,
                height=height * rows,
                linked=False,
                viewergrid=(rows, 2),
            )

    for i, (struct, title, subtitle, title_extra, subtitle_extra) in enumerate(
        zip_longest(structs, titles, subtitles, titles_extra, subtitles_extra)
    ):
        # Set the title and subtitle
        if isinstance(struct, list):
            name = struct[0].ids.name
        else:
            name = struct.ids.name

        title = f"{title or name or ''}"
        title_extra = f"{title_extra or ''}"
        subtitle = f"{subtitle or ''}"
        subtitle_extra = f"{subtitle_extra or ''}"

        if view_2d:
            if isinstance(struct, list):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Cannot display multiple 2D structures in one viewer. Do not submit"
                    " Structures in a list. If you want to view multiple structures, "
                    "unpack your list with *my_list_of_structures."
                )
            adjusted_width, adjusted_height = int(width * 0.75), int(height * 0.75)
            mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(struct.ids.smiles or structure_to_smiles(struct))
            img = Draw.MolToImage(mol, size=(adjusted_width, adjusted_height))
            buf = io.BytesIO()
            img.save(buf, format="PNG")
            img_str = base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode("utf-8")

            html_parts.append(
                f'<div style="margin: 10px; text-align: center; padding: 15px; width: '
                f'{adjusted_width}px; height: {adjusted_height + 60}px;">'
                f"<h2>{title} {title_extra}</h2>"
                f'<img src="data:image/png;base64,{img_str}" width="{adjusted_width}" '
                f'height="{adjusted_height}"/>'
                f"<h4>{subtitle} {subtitle_extra}</h4>"
                f"</div>"
            )
        else:
            if same_viewer:
                # No grid for single viewer (better performance than (1,1) grid)
                viewer_kwargs = {}
            else:
                # Sets the viewer to the correct grid position
                viewer_kwargs = {"viewer": divmod(i, 2)}

            if isinstance(struct, list):  # Animate lists of structures
                combined_xyz = "".join(s.to_xyz() for s in struct)
                viewer.addModelsAsFrames(combined_xyz, "xyz", **viewer_kwargs)
                viewer.animate(
                    {"loop": "forward", "interval": interval}, **viewer_kwargs
                )
            else:
                viewer.addModel(struct.to_xyz(), "xyz", **viewer_kwargs)

            viewer.addLabel(
                f"{title} {title_extra}",
                {
                    "position": {"x": width / 2, "y": 0, "z": 0},
                    "alignment": "topCenter",
                    "fontSize": 24,
                    "backgroundOpacity": 0,
                    "fontColor": "black",
                    "useScreen": True,
                },
                **viewer_kwargs,
            )

            viewer.addLabel(
                f"{subtitle} {subtitle_extra}",
                {
                    "position": {"x": width / 2, "y": height, "z": 0},
                    "alignment": "bottomCenter",
                    "fontSize": 20,
                    "backgroundOpacity": 0,
                    "fontColor": "black",
                    "useScreen": True,
                },
                **viewer_kwargs,
            )
            if distances:
                assert isinstance(struct, Structure), (
                    "Displaying distances for lists of structures is not yet implemented"
                )
                for atom1, atom2 in distances:
                    a1_coords = struct.geometry_angstrom[atom1]
                    a2_coords = struct.geometry_angstrom[atom2]
                    # Add line between the two atoms
                    viewer.addLine(
                        {
                            "start": {
                                "x": a1_coords[0],
                                "y": a1_coords[1],
                                "z": a1_coords[2],
                            },
                            "end": {
                                "x": a2_coords[0],
                                "y": a2_coords[1],
                                "z": a2_coords[2],
                            },
                            "color": "red",
                            "linewidth": 2,
                        },
                        **viewer_kwargs,
                    )
                    # Add a label showing the distance
                    midpoint = (a1_coords + a2_coords) / 2
                    distance = struct.distance(atom1, atom2, units=length_unit)
                    unit = "a₀"

                    if length_unit == LengthUnit.ANGSTROM:
                        unit = "Å"

                    viewer.addLabel(
                        f"{distance:.2f} {unit}",
                        {
                            "position": {
                                "x": midpoint[0],
                                "y": midpoint[1],
                                "z": midpoint[2],
                            },
                            "backgroundColor": "white",
                            "fontSize": 14,
                            "fontColor": "black",
                        },
                        **viewer_kwargs,
                    )

            if show_indices:
                ang_geom = (
                    struct.geometry_angstrom
                    if not isinstance(struct, list)
                    else struct[0].geometry_angstrom
                )
                for j, coord in enumerate(ang_geom):
                    viewer.addLabel(
                        str(j),
                        {"position": {"x": coord[0], "y": coord[1], "z": coord[2]}},
                        **viewer_kwargs,
                    )

    if not view_2d:
        viewer.setStyle(style or {"stick": {}, "sphere": {"scale": 0.3}})
        viewer.zoomTo()
        html_parts.append(f"{viewer.write_html()}")

    html_parts.append("</div>")
    return "".join(html_parts)

def generate_output_table(*results: ProgramOutput) -> str:
    """Generate an HTML table displaying the basic parameters for ProgramOutput objects.

    Args:
        *results: The ProgramOutput objects to display.

    Returns:
        str: A string of HTML displaying the ProgramOutput objects in a table.
    """
    styles = """
    <style>
        table {
            border-collapse: collapse;
            width: 100%;
        }
        th, td {
            border: 1px solid black;
            padding: 8px;
            text-align: left;
        }
        .inner-table {
            border: none;
            width: 100%;
        }
        .inner-table td {
            border: none;
            padding: 2px 5px;
        }
        .key, .value {
            text-align: left;
            white-space: nowrap;
        }
    </style>
    """

    table_header = """
    <table>
        <tr>
            <th>Structure</th>
            <th>Success</th>
            <th>Wall Time</th>
            <th>Calculation Type</th>
            <th>Requested Program</th>
            <th>Result Program</th>
            <th>Model</th>
            <th>Keywords</th>
    """
    has_files = any(res.input_data.files for res in results)
    has_subprograms = any(
        isinstance(res.input_data, ProgramInput) and res.input_data.subprograms
        for res in results
    )
    if has_files:
        table_header += "<th>Input Files</th>"

    if has_subprograms:
        table_header += "<th>Subprograms</th>"
    table_header += "</tr>"

    table_rows = []
    for res in results:
        structured = (
            res.input_data if isinstance(res.input_data, ProgramInput) else None
        )
        subject = None
        if structured is not None:
            subject = structured.structure or structured.initial_chain[0]
        success_style = (
            'style="color: green; font-weight: bold;"'
            if res.success
            else 'style="color: red; font-weight: bold;"'
        )
        base_row = f"""
        <tr>
            <td>{
            generate_dictionary_string(
                {
                    "charge": subject.charge,
                    "multiplicity": subject.multiplicity,
                    "name": subject.ids.name or "",
                }
            )
            if subject
            else ""
        }</td>
            <td {success_style}>{res.success}</td>
            <td> {
            _format_time(res.execution.wall_time)
            if res.execution.wall_time is not None
            else "No timing data"
        }</td>
            <td>{structured.calctype if structured else ""}</td>
            <td>{html.escape(res.input_data.program)}</td>
            <td>{
            f"{res.results.provenance.program} {res.results.provenance.program_version or ''}"
        }</td>
            <td>{
            generate_dictionary_string(
                structured.model.model_dump(exclude={"extras", "qcdata_version"})
            )
            if structured and structured.model
            else ""
        }</td>
            <td>{
            generate_dictionary_string(structured.keywords) if structured else ""
        }</td>
        """
        if has_files:
            base_row += f"<td>{generate_files_string(res.input_data.files)}</td>"

        if has_subprograms:
            base_row += f"<td>{generate_subprograms_string(structured.subprograms) if structured else ''}</td>"
        base_row += "</tr>"
        table_rows.append(base_row)

    table_footer = "</table>"
    return styles + table_header + "\n".join(table_rows) + table_footer

def generate_optimization_plot(
    prog_output: ProgramOutput,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (6.4, 4.8),
    grid: bool = True,
) -> str:
    """Generate a plot of the energy optimization by cycle for a single ProgramOutput.

    Args:
        prog_output: The ProgramOutput to generate the plot for.
        figsize: The size of the figure in inches.
        grid: Whether to display grid lines on the plot.

    Returns:
        str: A string of HTML displaying the plot as a png image encoded in base64.
    """
    energies = prog_output.results.energies * constants.HARTREE_TO_KCAL_PER_MOL
    if not energies.size or not np.isfinite(energies).any():
        return "<p>No optimization energies available.</p>"
    baseline_energy = energies[0]
    relative_energies = energies - baseline_energy
    last_is_nan = np.isnan(relative_energies[-1])

    if last_is_nan:
        try:
            delta_E = relative_energies[-2]
        except IndexError:
            # If there is only one energy point, set delta_E to nan
            delta_E = np.nan
    else:
        delta_E = relative_energies[-1]

    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    color = "tab:blue"
    ax1.set_xlabel("Optimization Cycle")
    ax1.set_ylabel("Relative Energy (kcal/mol)", color=color)
    ax1.plot(relative_energies, label="Energy", marker="o", color="green")
    if last_is_nan:
        ax1.plot(len(relative_energies) - 1, delta_E, marker="x", color="red")
    ax1.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor=color)
    ax1.text(
        0.95,
        0.85,
        f"ΔE = {delta_E:.2f} kcal/mol",
        verticalalignment="top",
        horizontalalignment="right",
        transform=ax1.transAxes,
        color="black",
        fontsize=14,
    )
    plt.title("Energy Optimization by Cycle", pad=20)
    ax1.legend(loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.95))

    buf = io.BytesIO()
    plt.savefig(buf, format="png", bbox_inches="tight")
    buf.seek(0)
    image_base64 = base64.b64encode(buf.read()).decode("utf-8")
    buf.close()
    plt.close(fig)  # Close the figure to avoid duplicate plots
    return (
        f'<img src="data:image/png;base64,{image_base64}" alt="Energy Optimization by '
        f'Cycle" style="width: 100%; max-width: {DEFAULT_WIDTH}px;">'
    )

docs.title: Wavefunctions in qcdata
docs.text: What qcdata returns about a calculation's wavefunction, and why. This is output data. Programs keep their internal structures and their warm-start state: the standardized wavefunction is not a restart format (a tight-binding program warm-starts from its multipole moments and densities, an SCF program from its own copy of the orbitals, inside a session). Given orbitals (ProgramInput.given) may at most seed a guess.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• One home for every number.
  • Store what cannot be derived. The SCF density is C n Cᵀ of the returned orbitals (Orbitals.density()); AO integrals that any integral library recomputes from the basis wait for a consumer.
  • A field arrives with a consumer and a definition two programs can test.
  • Models always hold arrays; only saving decides between inline JSON and a file.
  • TREXIO: the same physics and names where they agree; our own layout.

docs.title: Orbitals: the one home of the orbital levels
docs.text:
field meaning spin restricted: one coefficient matrix, one set of energies, one Hamiltonian, occupations per spin. unrestricted: everything per spin kind enum. canonical: eigenvectors of hamiltonian, energies required. natural: eigenvectors of a density, occupations, no energies. localized: no energies; localization names the method. Values are added when a program produces them energies_a/_b Eh; _b only for unrestricted orbitals occupations_a/_b both always, each between 0 and 1 electronic_temperature K; 0 for aufbau occupations fermi_level_a/_b Eh; None at 0 K, both given above it except for a spin that holds no electrons, which has none. Open shells are filled per spin at fixed n_α and n_β, so there are two core_electrons one per atom: the electrons the orbitals do not represent, ECP cores or the core a valence-only method leaves out (bookkeeping only; Zn's core is 28 in GFN2 and g-xTB). None: all-electron coefficients_a/_b optional, nao × nmo, in the AOs of Wavefunction.basis; only on request (output orbitals)
  • Tight binding's open shells (GFN2-xTB) are restricted orbitals of one spin-averaged Hamiltonian with per-spin occupations. They are not ROHF.
  • Levels and coefficients are separate because their costs differ. Levels are free and wanted on every frame of an optimization; coefficients cost time (GFN2-xTB on (H₂O)₂₀₀: an energy and gradient take 3.4 s without them, 4.9 s with) and nao × nmo numbers per spin (caffeine in def2-SVP: 246 energies against 60,516 coefficients).
  • core_electrons lives with the levels, not the basis set, so the electron count can be checked on every frame, coefficients or not. All-electron producers write nothing; tight-binding programs give their valence-only cores (no ECP involved), and on every ECP atom it equals the ECP's own core_electrons.
  • Where the structure is known (a ProgramOutput or a Frame), core_electrons lists its atoms and the occupations add up to Σ(Z − core_electrons) − charge, to 1e-6 electrons. This checks electron populations, not charges: g-xTB 2.0.1's reference occupations are not integers, so its charges for a neutral molecule sum to −7e-10. A given wavefunction (ProgramInput.given) may come from another charge or multiplicity, so only its atoms are checked.
  • density() raises a clear error when coefficients are missing, as Molden export does.
  • Orbitals holds no basis set. The basis set describes the AO space that the coefficients and every AO matrix share, so it belongs to their common parent, Wavefunction.basis. An overlap requested alone then ships no coefficients, which for unrestricted orbitals would be twice the overlap's own size.

docs.title: BasisSet
docs.text:
• shells and ao_convention. Tight-binding orbitals fit this layout exactly: GFN2-xTB and g-xTB orbitals are orthonormal to 4e-15–8e-15 in an independently computed overlap, and their spherical coefficients map onto their Cartesian ones to 1e-16.
  • ecp: a list of Ecp(center, core_electrons, local: list[EcpTerm], semilocal: list[list[EcpTerm]]), at most one per atom. semilocal[l], for l = 0..L−1, is the channel U_l − U_L, as Basis Set Exchange, NWChem, PySCF and Psi4 store it. EcpTerm(power, exponent, coefficient) is coefficient · r^power · exp(−exponent r²). power is the power of r (−2 or more): Basis Set Exchange JSON and NWChem write n for r^(n−2), so their converters subtract 2. Scalar ECPs only; spin-orbit terms are refused.
  • An ECP carries the number of core electrons it replaces, as Basis Set Exchange, NWChem, PySCF and Psi4 keep it with the potential, so a basis set alone (one built for an input, or one in given) is a complete potential and converts to another program without the orbitals. Orbitals.core_electrons keeps, per atom, what the orbitals leave out, which is more than the ECPs for a valence-only method; a Wavefunction checks that the two agree on every ECP atom.
  • A basis belongs to one geometry. GFN2's is the same per element at any geometry. g-xTB's q-vSZP contraction depends on each atom's EEQ-BC charge and coordination number at that geometry (fixed during the SCF), so the frames of a g-xTB trajectory do not share a BasisSet. g-xTB's scaled-exponent H0 basis is internal; the wavefunction's basis is the SCF basis.

docs.title: Wavefunction: the basis set and AO matrices, on request
docs.text:
basis is present whenever coefficients or an AO matrix are, and only then: it is the AO space they share, in its AOConvention. Each AO matrix is requested by its output name, the field's (overlap, hamiltonian, core_hamiltonian); the conventions list what each implies. overlap and core_hamiltonian imply only the basis set; hamiltonian implies overlap and orbitals.

field HF and DFT tight binding overlap yes yes: the program's own S, with its screening hamiltonian_a/_b Fock or Kohn-Sham matrix tight-binding Hamiltonian core_hamiltonian yes — (tight binding's H0 is model data)
  • A Wavefunction always has orbitals; GFN-FF and other force fields return none.
  • A hamiltonian comes with overlap and the orbitals' coefficients, and H C = S C ε holds with the returned S only: a screened S (a tight-binding program skips distant primitive pairs) can differ from an exact one by up to 3.4e-9. Its orbitals are canonical, and restricted orbitals have one Hamiltonian.
  • core_hamiltonian is every density-independent one-electron term of the run: T, V_ne with charges Z − core_electrons, V_ecp, and external point charges and fields once a program supports them. tr(P h), with P the density of the SCF's last input, is energy_components' one_electron term. With P = Orbitals.density(), the density a reader has, the two agree only to the SCF residual, as for the hamiltonian: compare them at SCF tolerance, never at round-off.
  • Every matrix is nao × nao of basis, and the coefficients have one row per AO of it; an AO-indexed array without a basis set, or a basis set without one, is refused.
  • Wavefunction.with_convention converts the coefficients and every matrix together, each with its variance: coefficients scale by s per AO index, densities by s_μ s_ν, operators (S, H, h) by 1/(s_μ s_ν). A spherical reordering is a permutation either way; a change of Cartesian normalization is not, so the coefficient transform does not apply to matrices. BasisSet.transform takes the array's kind (coefficients, operator, density) and never guesses it. Large arrays are converted as arrays, never through Python lists.

docs.title: The Hamiltonian
docs.text:
hamiltonian is the operator of one build at the last build's input x (a density, or tight binding's charges and multipole moments), however that input was mixed. The returned orbitals are its fresh generalized eigenvectors with the returned S, so H C = S C ε holds to rounding (max |CᵀHC − diag ε| below 1e-13 for an exact build).

  • Allowed: mixing inputs (Broyden or DIIS on moments, damping of densities).
  • Not allowed: combining several builds' operators (DIIS on F or H), damping or level shifting the returned matrix, or returning H and C from different iterations.
  • Requesting hamiltonian changes no other returned number.
  • H is F[x], not F of C n Cᵀ: the returned orbitals' density is one step ahead, and the two differ by the SCF residual (1.2e-6–1.6e-6 for caffeine at default thresholds).

How SCF schemes meet the rule:

scheme what the program does HF/DFT, F rebuilt from the last density and diagonalized the final build is always complete, never incremental. Against an incremental final build this moves energies by about 1e-11 Eh and orbital energies by up to 3e-9, and costs about 6% of the time for CPU energies with exact J/K, within the timing noise GFN2-xTB, mixers on input moments nothing: H is one build g-xTB 1.1, ending with one unmixed iteration nothing DIIS on the Fock matrix (g-xTB 2.0.1) one unmixed iteration after convergence: one more iteration, 3–4% more time, and closer to convergence in all 14 cases measured (taxol's energy error against tight thresholds: 1.2e-7 → 2.6e-8 Eh); results move by up to 1e-7 Eh and 4e-5 Eh/bohr a mode that must reproduce another program's numbers exactly, and so keeps its DIIS rule refuses a hamiltonian request (not_applicable) a composite (a solvation model on a base method) returns its base part's wavefunction; record names it; H and P do not reproduce the composite energy a force field wavefunction is None

What H contains:

  • DFT: everything in the SCF operator: V_xc on the run's final grid, plus VV10's nonlocal potential; range-separated exchange; J/K as built (density-fitted when the program fits, COSX K on its final grid); the PCM operator. Nothing for D3/D4 or SMD's CDS term, which do not depend on the density.
  • Tight binding: GFN2: H0 plus the potentials of the last input moments (shell, multipole, third order). g-xTB: the unmixed Fock matrix at the last input.

docs.title: Populations and multipoles (SinglePointData)
docs.text:
• shell_populations: electron populations Σ_{μ∈shell}(PS)_μμ, indexed like Wavefunction.basis.shells, with shell_atoms and shell_angular_momenta so they stand without a basis (and must match its shells when there is one). Not charges, which depend on method-specific reference occupations.
  • atomic_spin_populations: n_α − n_β per atom, with atomic_spin_populations_kind naming the partition from the values of atomic_charges_kind.
  • atomic_dipoles, atomic_quadrupoles: the electronic part only, about each atom (μ_A = −Σ_{μ∈A}(P D)_μμ, integrals about the column AO's atom); quadrupoles Buckingham traceless (3/2 M − 1/2 tr M), 3 × 3 per atom.
  • quadrupole_moment is the Buckingham traceless tensor, with no kind beside it. tblite's molecular quadrupole, which the g-xTB 2.0.1 program prints, counts the off-diagonal charge and dipole parts twice and is not a tensor.

docs.title: Deferred until a consumer is named
docs.text: data why it waits kinetic, potential_n_e, ecp_potential, dipole_integrals programs could fill them, but any integral library recomputes them from the basis and ECP in milliseconds, and each is a definition two programs must test solvent_potential H already contains the solvent operator and record names the model; for tight binding, removing it gives no gas-phase answer stored densities only for densities that are not C n Cᵀ of the returned orbitals (relaxed, response, or a mixed density returned without orbitals), with a kind (scf, relaxed, unrelaxed) two-electron integrals, DF and Cholesky tensors tight binding has none; a 3-index DF tensor is about 200 GB at 2000 functions. For CC or QMC: MO-basis Cholesky vectors of an active space, exported to TREXIO, on demand tight-binding kernels and H0, DFT grids and response intermediates, GFN2's Slater exponents specific to one model or one program, or not the functions the program computes with

docs.title: Large arrays
docs.text:
• Models always hold arrays. No field is ever a file reference: that would make equality, hashing, pickling to workers and moving a result between hosts depend on files beside it. Lazy loading is the reader's business.
  • Saving decides by float64 size: an array of more than 1 MiB (131,072 numbers; square matrices from nao ≥ 363) goes to a file beside the JSON, so the same result always saves the same way. Caffeine in def2-SVP stays inline; def2-TZVP does not.
  • Each such array is its own .npy file beside the saved file, named by the file's stem and the field path (output.results.wavefunction.orbitals.coefficients_a.npy): little-endian float64, C order, uncompressed (compression saves about 4% on coefficients). The JSON holds a pointer in its place with the file's path, the shape, the dtype and the file's sha256.
  • Inline floats round-trip exactly.
  • JSON costs 21.8–23.2 bytes per float64, against 8 in binary. A 2000-function matrix is 32 MB binary and 87–93 MB as JSON (1.2 s in json.dumps).

docs.title: TREXIO
docs.text:
The same physics and names; our own layout. A converter in qcinf, built on the trexio package (an optional extra), writes real TREXIO files, tested by a round trip: orbitals → TREXIO → PySCF energy at the same density.

TREXIO qcdata nucleus.* Structure basis.* (flat per-primitive arrays; shell_factor × prim_factor × coefficient) Wavefunction.basis.shells (per-atom Shell, one normalization convention) ecp.* BasisSet.ecp (local and semilocal channels; power of r; z_core as Ecp.core_electrons), Orbitals.core_electrons ao.cartesian, ao.normalization Shell.pure, AOConvention (spherical_order="trexio" selectable, never the default) ao_1e_int.overlap, core_hamiltonian Wavefunction.overlap, core_hamiltonian ao_1e_int.kinetic, potential_n_e, ecp, dipole deferred mo.coefficient [mo, ao], mo.spin Orbitals.coefficients_a/_b [ao, mo] mo.energy, mo.occupation, mo.type, mo.electronic_temperature energies_*, occupations_* (per spin, 0..1, where TREXIO keeps one occupation per orbital: the converter checks whether a restricted file's are totals, 0..2), kind, electronic_temperature — fermi_level_a/_b rdm.1e_up/_dn (MO basis) Orbitals.density() (AO basis, computed) — (no Fock matrix) hamiltonian_a/_b ao_2e_int, mo_2e_int, determinant, amplitude, jastrow, qmc not in qcdata

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Being able to quickly and easily visualize results is critical for efficient scientific work. qcdata come with build-in visualizations for all objects.

Install the visualization module and its required dependencies:

python -m pip install qcdata[view]

OR

python -m pip install qcdata[all]

Then in a Jupyter Notebook import the view module and call view.view(...) on any Structure or ProgramOutput object to instantly visualize your results. Click on the examples on the left to see this in action ✨!
